baseline.description:
`rebar list --type=<t>` only matches a single type. Passing a comma-separated list (e.g. `--type=task,story`) returns `[]` (no matches) rather than the union of the two types.

Contrast with --status, --priority, --has-tag, and --without-tag, whose help text explicitly documents comma-separated OR semantics. --type silently does not, so a caller expecting OR semantics gets an empty result with no error — the most confusing failure mode.

Acceptance criteria:
- `rebar list --status=open --type=task,story` returns the union of open tasks and open stories (not []).
- Behavior matches the OR semantics already used by --status/--priority/--has-tag.
- --type help text documents the comma-separated OR behavior.
- Unit/interface test covers the multi-type case.

Repro:
  rebar list --status=open --type=task,story   # -> [] today; should be union
  rebar list --status=open --type=task          # -> N tasks
  rebar list --status=open --type=story          # -> M stories

Discovered while listing parentless open task/story tickets (had to query each type separately and merge with jq).
baseline.summary: list --type does not accept a comma-separated list of types

baseline.description:
## What
One-time backfill of `close_class` for already-closed bugs that lack it, inferred from STRUCTURAL signals only (no prose recovery, no LLM guessing): a bug whose reduced `reverts` contains a revert of a STATUS/COMMITS event → `regression`; a bug with a plan-review `BLOCK` in its `REVIEW_RESULT` history → `plan_defect`; a bug with a `gate_error_v1` ERROR on its sidecar streams → `env_integration`; otherwise → `undetermined`. Every backfilled value is labeled and segregated from authoritative going-forward `--class` values.

## Data-access ground truth (the plan is built on this)
- **Only backfill bugs where `state["close_class"]` is ABSENT** (a bug already closed with `--class` keeps its authoritative value; `close_class` is folded on the `*→closed` edge, `_processors.py:195-209`). Reduce via `reduce_ticket`.
- **REVERT signal**: reduced `state["reverts"]` is a list of `{target_event_uuid, target_event_type, timestamp, ...}` (`_processors.py:452-462`) — a revert of a SPECIFIC prior event of ANY type. A "regression" inference requires a revert whose `target_event_type` is `STATUS` or `COMMITS` (a substantive revert), not a revert of a COMMENT/LINK.
- **plan-review BLOCK signal**: `REVIEW_RESULT` events are reducer-ignored (`_version.py:77`) and NOT in compiled state — read them via `rebar.llm.plan_review.sidecar.all_review_results(id, repo_root=)` (returns retained payloads; check `verdict=="BLOCK"`). (Retention caps at 50/ticket, so a very old BLOCK may be pruned — an accepted best-effort limit, logged.)
- **env_integration signal**: a `gate_error_v1` ERROR record on the bug's `REVIEW_RESULT`/`COMPLETION_VERDICT` streams. This MUST use a **raw event-file scan** (NOT `all_review_results`, whose schema guard accepts only `plan_review_result_v1/v2` and silently skips `gate_error_v1`): resolve the ticket dir (`tracker_dir`+`resolve_ticket_dir_name`), glob `*-REVIEW_RESULT.json` AND `*-COMPLETION_VERDICT.json`, `json.load` each, and check `event["data"].get("schema") == "gate_error_v1"` — mirroring the `scan_event_payloads` helper in `tests/unit/workflow/test_gate_error_sidecar.py`. (The plan-review BLOCK signal above CAN use `all_review_results` since a BLOCK is a `plan_review_result_v2` payload; only the gate_error scan needs the raw path.)
- These signals are **heuristic evidence, not proof**: the structural facts (a REVERT of a STATUS event; a BLOCK verdict; an ERROR record) are reliable, but the class they imply is an inference. Anything not confidently inferable → `undetermined` (the explicit escape bucket in `CLOSE_CLASSES`).

## The backfill artifact (concrete target + idempotency)
Backfilled classifications are written as one JSON object per line to a dedicated, git-TRACKED NDJSON file **`.rebar/backfill-close-class.ndjson`** — a *separate* artifact from the authoritative STATUS-folded `close_class`, so backfilled values are never confused with (or aggregated into) authoritative ones. Because `.gitignore` blanket-ignores `.rebar/*` (line 20) with per-file negations, the script's Files list includes a `.gitignore` edit adding `!.rebar/backfill-close-class.ndjson` (mirroring `!.rebar/criteria_routing.json`) so the artifact persists.
- **Record shape:** `{"ticket_id", "close_class", "source": "backfill_classified", "confidence": "classified", "evidence": "<which signal fired>", "ts": "<ISO-8601>"}`.
- **Idempotency (precise mechanism):** the script first reads the existing artifact and builds the set of already-recorded `ticket_id`s; it SKIPS any bug already present in that set AND any bug whose reduced `state["close_class"]` is set (authoritative). So re-running appends nothing new for already-processed bugs — idempotent by `ticket_id`. `--dry-run` prints the classifications without writing.

## Files
- `scripts/backfill_bug_class.py` — new standalone script (per the above): classify closed bugs lacking `close_class`, append labeled records to `.rebar/backfill-close-class.ndjson`, idempotent by `ticket_id`, `--dry-run` supported.
- `.gitignore` — add `!.rebar/backfill-close-class.ndjson` (past the blanket `.rebar/*` ignore) so the artifact is tracked.
- `tests/scripts/test_backfill_bug_class.py` — new (tier `tests/scripts/`, `pytestmark = pytest.mark.scripts` — NOT the nonexistent `tests/unit/scripts/`).

## Approach
The original free-text reasons were discarded, so only structural signals are trustworthy. Classifying solely from REVERT / plan-review BLOCK / gate ERROR linkage (and `undetermined` for everything else) keeps the backfill honest and avoids contamination. Every backfilled record carries `source=backfill_classified, confidence=classified` so the c085 registry keeps them apart from authoritative structural series (`is_authoritative("backfill_classified")` is False).

## Tests
- Unit (`tests/scripts/`, real temp store; craft closed bugs with the signals): a bug with a REVERT of a STATUS event → `regression`; a bug with a `REVIEW_RESULT` BLOCK → `plan_defect`; a bug with a `gate_error_v1` ERROR → `env_integration`; a plain closed bug with none → `undetermined`; a bug already carrying `close_class` is SKIPPED (not re-backfilled). Every emitted record carries `source=backfill_classified` + `confidence=classified`.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] `tests/scripts/test_backfill_bug_class.py` passes (tier `scripts`): the four fixtures classify to `regression`, `plan_defect`, `env_integration`, `undetermined` respectively (exact-value asserts on the emitted record's `close_class`).
- [ ] a bug that already has `state["close_class"]` is NOT overwritten/re-emitted (idempotence + authoritative-value protection) — asserted.
- [ ] every backfilled record carries `source=="backfill_classified"` and `confidence=="classified"`, and `is_authoritative(record.source)` is False — asserted on the output, proving segregation from authoritative series.
- [ ] a REVERT whose only `target_event_type` is `COMMENT` does NOT yield `regression` (it falls through to `undetermined`) — asserted, proving the substantive-revert filter.
baseline.summary: Backfill historical bug --class from structural signals only

content.text: ## Why
The cross-cutting requirement is ONE shared registry consumed by all gates. The risky core is
already shared (`review_kernel/` verify/decide/coach — both gates consume it). But the
registry/descriptor layer is duplicated: plan-review has `load_criteria()` (a merged descriptor);
code-review (`b744`) has only `routing_index()` (raw routing, no descriptor loader, no
`facet/checklist`, and a **deliberately divergent** `blocking_enabled` vs `default_posture`). This story unifies them into `rebar.llm.criteria`. **b744 has LANDED on `main`** (PR #102), so
`code_review/` is available and this capstone is now workable.
## What
- Introduce `rebar.llm.criteria`: the shared merged-descriptor abstraction + loader both gates
consume (generalize plan-review's `load_criteria`; give code-review the descriptor it lacks).
- Reconcile the **deliberate** posture divergence in one `threshold_for` that honors BOTH
`default_posture` (plan-review) and `blocking_enabled` (code-review) — do NOT "fix" the
divergence away.
- Exec-tier-polymorphic criteria: LLM overlays (prompt+contract+routing) AND prompt-less DET
invariants (the 2 security keys live only in code-review's `criteria_routing.json` today).
- Route code-review's `OVERLAY_IDS` / `routing_index` / `threshold_for` through the shared
`effective_criteria` so code-review also gets project criteria + the `.rebar/` overlay.
- **Preserve `review_code` / `code_review/shim.py`'s `review_result` return shape** — a
back-compat surface consumed by MCP `review_code`, CLI `rebar review-code`, and the Gerrit
`review_bot/adapter.py`.
- Docs/ADR: the how-to for authoring/activating/eval'ing/blocking on a criterion across gates.
## Scope
- Files: new `src/rebar/llm/criteria/` (shared); `src/rebar/llm/plan_review/registry.py` +
`code_review/registry.py` (delegate to it); `code_review/` attestation port.
- Migration is expand-contract; rollback = fail-open to packaged (overlay absent ⇒ both gates
behave as today). A misbehaving unified registry falls back per-gate.
- BLOCKED ON `b744` (epic `3156` already `depends_on b744`).
## Scope-narrowing + threshold_for design (remediation, run 1)
### Coherent single concern (clears G5 — no child decomposition)
This story is the **shared registry layer + posture reconciliation + docs** — ONE concern. The
cross-gate **attestation port** (`attest.py` → code-review + code-review `registry_version`) is
explicitly OWNED BY STORY `08af` (the attestation/invalidation story), NOT duplicated here; and
the DET-invariant consumer generalization is story `7f0d`. So the AC set below is the unification
core only (≤6 ACs, one architectural seam), not an epic-of-epics.
### `threshold_for` gate-dispatch (clears E2)
The unified `threshold_for(criteria, *, gate)` takes a **`gate` argument** (`"plan_review"` |
`"code_review"`) and applies that gate's OWN blocking convention over the SAME shared routing
records — it does NOT collapse the divergence:
- `gate="plan_review"` → a criterion blocks when its `default_posture == "blocking"`;
- `gate="code_review"` → a criterion blocks when its explicit `blocking_enabled` is true.
Both read `block_threshold` the same way (min over the criteria). Each gate's existing call site
passes its own `gate`, so neither gate's behaviour changes; the shared function just hosts both
conventions side-by-side (the deliberate posture divergence is preserved, per design).
## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] A shared `rebar.llm.criteria` layer that both plan-review and code-review consume, replacing
the two parallel registries.
- [ ] `threshold_for` honors BOTH posture conventions (`default_posture` + `blocking_enabled`)
without collapsing the divergence.
- [ ] The shared descriptor is exec-tier-polymorphic (LLM overlay + prompt-less DET).
- [ ] Code-review consumes `effective_criteria` (project criteria + `.rebar/` overlay work in
code-review too).
- [ ] `review_code` / `shim.py` `review_result` return shape is preserved (MCP + CLI + Gerrit).
- [ ] An ADR + `CLAUDE.md`/`docs/` how-to documents the unified registry across gates.

baseline.summary: Unify plan-review + code-review into shared rebar.llm.criteria (blocked on b744)

baseline.description:
## Context / Problem
`rebar review-plan --source local` is documented — in the CLI's own generated help — as
"local: read the in-place checkout (dirty allowed, **never signs**)". It signs.

A local-source PASS mints a fully CERTIFIED, CLAIM-VALID plan-review attestation. Probed on
origin/main (20ae67c61):

    signed=True source='local' verified_at_sha=None
    claim_gate_check -> ok=True reason='certified plan-review attestation'
    rebar claim       -> succeeds, ticket goes in_progress

That is a gate-integrity hole, not just a help-text drift. `--source local` reads the
IN-PLACE working tree, uncommitted edits included. So an agent can review a plan against
code that exists only in its dirty worktree and earn a claim attestation that binds
`verified_at_sha=None` — no committed SHA at all. The attested-snapshot discipline the
claim gate is built on (review a snapshot pinned at a ref, bind that SHA, re-hash the SAME
basis at claim time) is bypassed.

Discovered while writing boundary regression tests for epic 58f2-b6ed-363e-4608
(uninformed-aspiring-rhino), whose AC5 asserts "unattested local-source results remain
unsigned". They do not. Either the AC is wrong or the code is; this ticket resolves which.

## Reproduction Steps
1. Enable the claim gate: `[verify] require_plan_review_for_claim = true`.
2. Create an open, non-exempt ticket with a reviewable plan.
3. `rebar review-plan <id> --source local` (or library `review_plan(..., source="local")`)
   with a runner that yields a clean PASS.
4. Inspect the verdict: `signature.signed` is `True`, `verified_at_sha` is `None`.
5. `rebar claim <id>` — succeeds.

## Expected Behavior
One of the two, decided deliberately:
- **(A) Honor the documented contract:** a `source=local` review NEVER signs. It returns a
  PASS with `signature.signed=False` and a machine-readable unsigned reason naming the
  local-source policy. The claim gate stays unsatisfied.
- **(B) Change the contract:** local-source signing is intentional; then the help, the
  guides, and `docs/plan-review-gate.md` must say so, and the attestation must still bind a
  committed SHA rather than `None`.

(A) is the recommendation: the whole point of `verified_at_sha` is that the claim gate
re-hashes the same committed basis, which a dirty worktree cannot provide.

## Actual Behavior
`source=local` signs a certified attestation with `verified_at_sha=None`, and the claim gate
accepts it.

## Approach
1. Add the local-source guard at the shared sign-on-PASS finalization seam in
   `rebar.llm.plan_review` (NOT at each caller), alongside the existing non-PASS/degraded
   refusals in `attest.sign_plan_review`.
2. Surface a machine-readable unsigned reason so a caller can tell "policy declined to sign"
   from "signing failed".
3. Pin it with a table-driven never-sign test covering BLOCK / INDETERMINATE / degraded /
   local-source / explicit `sign=False`.
4. Audit whether any existing attestation in the store was minted from a local-source review
   (`verified_at_sha is None` is the tell) and decide whether to invalidate.

Rejected: fixing only the help text — that documents a gate bypass instead of closing it.

## Scope
- `src/rebar/llm/plan_review/__init__.py`
- `src/rebar/llm/plan_review/attest.py`
- `tests/interfaces/lifecycle/test_plan_review_gate.py`
- `docs/plan-review-gate.md`

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] A `source=local` PASS returns `signature.signed is False` and a machine-readable
      unsigned reason naming the local-source policy; an interface test asserts both.
- [ ] After a `source=local` PASS, `attest.claim_gate_check(...)` reports `ok=False` and a
      subsequent `rebar claim` is BLOCKED (exit 1) with the ticket still `open`.
- [ ] `test_pass_verdict_carries_a_passing_signature` (which today reviews with
      `source="local"` and asserts a signature) is updated to use the attested source, so the
      suite no longer encodes the bypass as expected behavior.
- [ ] A table-driven never-sign test covers BLOCK, INDETERMINATE, degraded, local-source, and
      explicit `sign=False`.
- [ ] No signed attestation can carry `verified_at_sha=None`; a test asserts the invariant.
- [ ] `docs/plan-review-gate.md` states the local-source never-signs rule.
- [ ] `make lint`, `make typecheck`, and the default non-integration pytest suite exit zero.
baseline.summary: review-plan --source local mints a claim-valid attestation despite documented 'never signs'

baseline.description:
## Reproduction Steps
1. Run `rebar review-plan <id>` (attested, signable) while ANY other rebar ticket-write is in flight (e.g. several concurrent background reviews, a waiter loop, another claim/edit) — enough contention to leave a stale/contended `$(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)/worktrees/-tickets-tracker/index.lock`.
2. The review runs its full multi-pass LLM pipeline (~8-12 min) and computes verdict=PASS, source=attested, signable=True.
3. The attestation SIGN step tries to commit the SIGNATURE event to the tickets branch and fails on the lock.

## Observed
The returned verdict dict is verdict=PASS with:
```
signature: {'signed': False, 'error': "Error: git commit failed while holding lock: fatal: Unable to create '.../.git/worktrees/-tickets-tracker/index.lock': File exists. Another git process seems to be running in this repository, or the lock file may be stale"}
```
The CLI exits 0 (PASS). But NO attestation is persisted on the ticket, so a subsequent `rebar claim <id>` FAILS the plan-review claim gate ('run the plan review to earn an attestation'). The only recovery is to re-run the ENTIRE ~10-min billable review. Observed live on ticket gnomish-nosophobic-arawana during epic jira-reb-687.

## Why this is major impact
- **Expensive, billable work is silently thrown away.** A full multi-pass LLM plan-review (minutes + real API cost) succeeds, but its sole durable product — the signed attestation that unlocks `claim` — is lost to a transient, recoverable git-lock condition.
- **Exit 0 + PASS masks the failure.** The signature failure is reported only inside `result.signature.error`; the process exits 0 and prints PASS, so an automated caller (or a human reading the verdict) reasonably believes the ticket is now claimable when it is not. The next `claim` fails confusingly ('no attestation') with no obvious link back to the swallowed sign error.
- **No cheap recovery path.** There is no way to re-persist the already-computed PASS verdict; you must re-run the whole review, doubling cost/latency and risking a DIFFERENT verdict on re-run (non-determinism).

## Root cause (direction)
The sign step commits the SIGNATURE event under the tickets-branch worktree index lock; a contended/stale `index.lock` makes `git commit` fail, and the failure is caught and recorded into `signature.error` but NOT (a) retried, (b) recovered by clearing a provably-stale lock, or (c) surfaced as a non-zero exit / loud CLI error. The attestation write is not resilient to the ordinary concurrency the rest of rebar's store already tolerates (writes auto-commit+auto-push under this lock constantly).

## Expected / graceful handling (design first)
- **Retry the signature commit** with bounded backoff on a lock/commit failure (the store's other writers already contend on this lock; the sign write should too).
- **Detect and clear a provably-stale `index.lock`** (no live git process / lock older than a threshold) before failing — the same recovery a human does by hand.
- **Fail LOUD, not silent**: if the verdict is PASS+signable but signing fails, the CLI should exit non-zero (or a distinct code) and print the sign error prominently — never exit 0/PASS while the attestation was NOT written.
- **Offer a cheap re-sign** of an already-computed, still-valid PASS verdict (persist the computed manifest so a follow-up `sign`/`review-plan` can re-attest without re-running all LLM passes) — so a transient lock costs a retry, not a full re-review.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] A signature-commit failure on a contended/stale lock is retried (bounded) and/or recovers by clearing a provably-stale lock; a transient lock no longer loses the attestation.
- [ ] When a PASS+signable review fails to persist its signature, the CLI exits NON-ZERO and prints the sign error prominently (no silent exit-0/PASS with an unwritten attestation).
- [ ] There is a cheap path to (re)persist the signature for an already-computed, still-valid PASS verdict without re-running the LLM passes.
- [ ] A regression test simulates a signature-commit failure and asserts (a) retry/recovery persists the attestation, or (b) a loud non-zero failure — never silent loss.
- [ ] make lint && make typecheck && make test green.
baseline.summary: plan-review computes PASS but silently loses the attestation when the signature commit fails (transient git index.lock) — expensive review wasted, claim still blocked

# Enforce the 50/72 commit-message rule with a local commit-msg hook

## Context / Problem

Gerrit renders a change description as preformatted text and preserves the author's newlines, so the wrapping a commit lands with is exactly what reviewers read (and what `git log` shows in an 80-column terminal). Gerrit's bundled `commit-message-length-validator` only WARNS (`warning: subject >50 characters`, `warning: too many message lines longer than 72 characters; manually wrap lines`), which is trivially ignored — and nothing in this repo checked it.

Result: commit bodies on `main` are split between hard-wrapped (72-79 col) and single-paragraph (129-286 col) styles. Measured with the new checker against the last 40 commits on origin/main: 5 pass, 35 fail, with failures like 177, 183, 222 and 223-char body lines. That inconsistency is what made the wrapping look like something rebar was doing to the text (investigated under ticket 368a, closed not_a_bug).

Research basis — all four major Gerrit-based projects mandate the same rule, and none avoids the line breaks:
- Go: "The text should be wrapped at around 72 columns" + "Don't use HTML, Markdown, or any other markup language."
- Chromium: "Long lines should be wrapped to 72 columns for easier log message viewing in terminals."
- ChromiumOS: "Wrap the body text to 72 characters so that `git log` looks nice"; subject ~60, 72 hard limit.
- Android: "Provide a long description that hard-wraps at 72 characters maximum"; subject 50 max.

## Approach

Enforce locally at commit time (operator's explicit choice: pre-commit framework, NOT CI).

- `scripts/check_commit_message_wrap.py` — check-only checker for the 50/72 rule, matching the repo's existing `scripts/check_*.py` convention. Never rewrites the message; it names the offending lines.
- Wired as a `commit-message-wrap` hook in `.pre-commit-config.yaml` at the **commit-msg** stage. It cannot run at the `pre-commit` stage because the commit message does not exist yet. `default_install_hook_types: [pre-commit, commit-msg]` installs both.
- `make hooks` now verifies BOTH hooks landed AND that Gerrit's Change-Id stamping survived.

Carve-outs (wrapping these would break them): trailers (`rebar-ticket:`, `Change-Id:`, `Signed-off-by:`), `TAG=` lines, fenced code blocks, indented literal blocks, table rows, and lines whose length comes from a single unsplittable atomic token (URL, path, dotted identifier). Comment lines and the `git commit --verbose` diff are ignored.

## Critical risk handled: Gerrit's commit-msg hook

Gerrit's own `commit-msg` hook (which stamps `Change-Id`) already owns that slot. `pre-commit install` defaults to MIGRATION mode, preserving the existing hook as `commit-msg.legacy` and running both. Verified empirically in a throwaway repo: a conforming commit still received its `Change-Id`; an over-long body was rejected and no commit was created. `pre-commit install -f/--overwrite` would delete Gerrit's hook and break every push — documented as a do-not-do in the config, the Makefile, and CONTRIBUTING.md, and `make hooks` warns if the Change-Id chain is missing.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] A commit whose body has a line over 72 columns is REJECTED locally, with output naming each offending line and its length.
- [ ] A commit whose subject exceeds 50 columns is REJECTED locally.
- [ ] A conforming commit succeeds AND still receives its Gerrit `Change-Id` trailer (Gerrit's hook is chained as `commit-msg.legacy`, not clobbered).
- [ ] A body line is EXEMPT from the 72-column check when any of these detection rules matches (each stated as the exact rule an executor implements):
  - [ ] **Trailer** — the stripped line matches `^[A-Za-z][A-Za-z0-9-]*:\s` (e.g. `rebar-ticket:`, `Change-Id:`, `Signed-off-by:`).
  - [ ] **Tag** — the stripped line matches `^[A-Z][A-Z0-9_]*=` (e.g. `BUG=`, `TEST=`).
  - [ ] **Fenced block** — the line lies between two lines matching `^\s*```{3}`; the fence marker TOGGLES, so prose after a closing fence is checked again.
  - [ ] **Indented literal block** — the RAW line begins with exactly 4+ spaces or a tab, i.e. `line.startswith(("    ", "\t"))`. A 1-3 space indent is NOT exempt.
  - [ ] **Table row** — the stripped line begins with `|`.
  - [ ] **Atomic token** — the line contains a whitespace-delimited token longer than 72 chars, EVERY such over-long token matches `://|[/\\]|\w[._-]\w` (a URL scheme, a path separator, or a dotted/underscored/hyphenated identifier), AND the rest of the stripped line (its length minus the longest such token) is itself <= 72. A 73+ char run of ordinary characters is NOT exempt.
- [ ] git's own scaffolding produces no false positives: comment (`#`) lines and the `git commit --verbose` diff below the `>8` marker are ignored.
- [ ] The checker never mutates the commit message (check-only, matching the repo's stated pre-commit policy).
- [ ] `.pre-commit-config.yaml` gains a top-level `default_install_hook_types: [pre-commit, commit-msg]` key, so the EXISTING bare `pre-commit install` in `make hooks` (which passes no `--hook-type`) installs both hook types with no flag change.
- [ ] The `hooks:` target in `Makefile` is MODIFIED to add the two new verification branches described below; it currently verifies only the `pre-commit` hook file and must not be left as-is.
- [ ] `make hooks` EXITS NON-ZERO when either the `pre-commit` or the `commit-msg` hook file is absent after install.
- [ ] `make hooks` prints a WARNING (and still exits zero) when no `Change-Id` stamping is found in `commit-msg` or `commit-msg.legacy`, since Gerrit's hook is fetched separately and its absence must not block wiring the local gates.
- [ ] CONTRIBUTING.md documents the enforcement, the exemption list, why the hook runs at the commit-msg stage, and the never-run-`pre-commit install -f` warning.
- [ ] Unit tests cover the rule, every carve-out, the fence-toggle case, and the CLI exit codes.

## Notes / scope

Local guardrail only — bypassable with `git commit --no-verify`, and CI does NOT check wrapping (deliberate: the operator chose pre-commit over CI). Existing history is not rewritten; the gate applies to new commits only.
baseline.summary: Enforce the 50/72 commit-message rule with a local commit-msg hook

## Context / Problem

Follow-up from fd71 (clayish-basaltine-bug), which wired the review bot to read `_usage` and emit token counts to CloudWatch — but only for the usage surfaced on the review's AGENT steps (Pass-2 `verify` + Pass-3 `decide`). The Pass-1 finder BATCH, often the largest token consumer, does not surface per-finder `_usage` on its batch step output: `src/rebar/llm/plan_review/production_batch_runner.py` emits `findings`/`criteria_count` (no `_usage`), and the shared `run_pass1` (`src/rebar/llm/plan_review/pass1.py`) returns only `findings`. So the CloudWatch token totals currently UNDERCOUNT by the finder pass.

## Approach

Aggregate each finder call's `_usage` inside `run_pass1` (each finder goes through `runner.run`, which attaches `_usage`) and thread a summed token dict up so the batch runner can place it on the `BatchRunResult.outputs` (e.g. `outputs['_usage']`). Then `finalize._attach_code_review_metrics` (and the plan-review metrics assembler) already sum `_usage` across steps, so finder tokens flow into `coverage['metrics']` automatically. This is a SHARED path (plan-review uses `run_pass1` too), so preserve the existing return contract carefully (add an out-param or extend the return tuple; behavior-preserving) and cover both gates.

## Scope

- Token counts only; no dollar cost.
- Must not change finder behavior, thresholds, or the plan-review path's outputs beyond adding the aggregated `_usage`.

## Testing

- Unit test that `run_pass1` returns/threads summed finder `_usage` and that the batch step output carries it.
- Unit test that `finalize` then includes finder tokens in `coverage['metrics']`.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] Pass-1 finder per-call `_usage` is aggregated and appears on the batch step output; verified by a unit test.
- [ ] `coverage['metrics']` token totals include finder usage after the change; verified by a finalize unit test.
- [ ] Both code-review and plan-review paths remain green; `make test`/`make lint`/`make typecheck` pass; lands via Gerrit with Verified +1 and LLM-Review +1.
baseline.summary: Surface Pass-1 finder token usage on the batch step output (complete review-bot token totals)

# Idea: self-hosted Renovate on Gerrit — peer-pattern dependency updates through the two gates

Captured 2026-07-09 during the OSS v1.0.0 front-door research (epic breaded-ammonitic-elephant). The APPROVED v1.0 design is Dependabot advisory PRs on the GitHub mirror (github-actions ecosystem only, monthly; PRs are unmergeable notifications the maintainer lands via Gerrit; lockdown bot exempts dependabot[bot]) — see story cardiac-lush-chihuahua. This idea records the researched alternative that would eliminate that departure from the Gerrit-peer pattern, for possible post-1.0 adoption.

## The finding

Renovate (Mend.io — the leading cross-platform dependency bot; what ruff/uv use) has a native self-hosted Gerrit platform (`platform=gerrit`, all Gerrit 3.x): it pushes each dependency bump directly as a **Gerrit Change** — no GitHub PRs — so updates flow through the same `LLM-Review` + `Verified` gates as human changes. That is the Wikimedia-LibraryUpgrader / OpenStack-requirements-bot pattern, off the shelf, and it matches rebar's dogfooding ethos (the dependency bot is just another contributor under the two-vote merge policy).

- Docs: https://docs.renovatebot.com/modules/platform/gerrit/ and https://docs.renovatebot.com/modules/platform/
- Mechanics: Gerrit bot account + HTTP credentials; SSH cloning supported (discussion #39625); metadata via a `Renovate-Branch` commit footer (needs Gerrit ≥3.6, satisfied); `autoApprove` exists but would stay OFF (our gates vote); `statusCheckNames` can map Renovate checks (e.g. minimumReleaseAge) onto Gerrit labels.

## Why it was NOT chosen for v1.0 (the blockers to re-evaluate)

1. **Experimental platform status**: Renovate's Gerrit support is officially experimental — maintainers deprioritize Gerrit issues and allow breaking changes in minor releases. Re-evaluate when it is declared stable.
2. **Ops cost**: Renovate is a CLI needing a scheduled runner (cron GitHub Action or the Gerrit host) plus credentials — a new moving part vs zero-ops Dependabot; disproportionate for a monthly, github-actions-only update stream.
3. **`rebar-ticket:` trailer integration**: the Verified gate requires a resolving rebar-ticket trailer on every commit; Renovate has a known open issue with commit trailers via `commitBody` on Gerrit (https://github.com/renovatebot/renovate/discussions/33306). Adoption needs one of: a working trailer config, a standing "dependency updates" ticket baked into the commit template, or a narrow bot exemption in the require-ticket check.
4. No Dependency Dashboard on Gerrit (built on Issues) — cosmetic at this scale.

## Promotion sketch (if/when picked up)

- Trial on a scratch Gerrit project first: bot account, `platform=gerrit`, github-actions manager only; verify trailer handling end-to-end through both gates; verify the LLM-Review bot behaves sanely on bot-authored changes.
- If adopted: retire the Dependabot advisory-PR flow (delete .github/dependabot.yml or reduce to security-alerts posture), remove the lockdown-bot dependabot exemption, and update the decision records in docs/releasing.md + the dependabot.yml rationale that story cardiac-lush-chihuahua created.
- Revisit triggers: Renovate Gerrit platform declared stable; dependency-update volume growing beyond monthly-actions-only (e.g. a committed uv.lock); the advisory-PR flow proving annoying in practice.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] (To be designed at promotion — this is a parked idea, not dispatchable work.)
baseline.summary: Self-hosted Renovate on Gerrit: peer-pattern dependency updates through the two gates (post-1.0)

content.text: The MCP tool and the Python library both pass a ticket_id to `validate`, but the
engine `validate` is REPO-WIDE and rejects positionals. Reproduced empirically.
- Engine: src/rebar/_engine/validate-issues.sh:81-84 — catch-all `*) echo "Unknown option: $1"; exit 1`.
- Library: src/rebar/__init__.py:197-203 — `validate(ticket_id, *, repo_root=None)` builds `["validate", ticket_id, "--json"]`. Signature REQUIRES ticket_id (cannot be called id-less -> TypeError).
- MCP: src/rebar/mcp_server.py:153-156 — `validate(ticket_id: str) -> dict`.
- Repro: `rebar validate <id>` -> `Unknown option: <id>`, exit 1; `rebar.validate('<id>')` -> {'output':'Unknown option: <id>','exit_code':1}; `rebar.validate()` -> TypeError.
## Fix

- Library: make validate repo-wide (no ticket_id); call `["validate","--json"]`; parse stdout JSON into the report dict. NOTE: validate's nonzero exit is score-encoded (exit = 5 - score), NOT an error — do not raise on nonzero; return the report.
- MCP: drop the ticket_id param (`def validate() -> dict`); update docstring.
- Update any existing tests that call validate with an id.
## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] `rebar.validate()` (no id) returns the repo-wide report dict {score,critical_issues,major_issues,minor_issues,warnings,suggestions}
- [ ] MCP `validate` tool takes no ticket_id and returns the report
- [ ] Score-encoded nonzero exit does not raise / is not treated as failure
- [ ] Test covers library + MCP repo-wide validate; existing id-passing tests updated

## Problem

Change 330c (commit 9ba1e90e3c, "box flips no longer stale attestations") normalizes AC checkbox STATE (case-insensitive x, - or * bullets, line-anchored) to '[ ]' before hashing the material fingerprint, so flipping boxes at close no longer stales a plan-review attestation or the completion-verifier staleness check. The commit touched only src/rebar/llm/plan_review/pass1.py + tests — no documentation.

docs/plan-review-gate.md still teaches the OLD behavior:

- §"Attestation, freshness & invalidation" (~L469): "the bound material fingerprint matches the current ticket — a material edit (description/AC/file-impact/decomposition) invalidates it. (Tags/comments/links/assignee are not material and do not invalidate.)" — a reader concludes any description edit, including box flips, invalidates. Checkbox-state flips are now explicitly NOT material.
- The close-gate flow describes the AC-checkbox completeness precheck (~L901) requiring boxes checked before close, with no note that checking them is fingerprint-safe — the exact author fear the 330c fix removed.

## Plan

Update docs/plan-review-gate.md:
1. In the invalidation list (~L469), extend the non-material parenthetical: checkbox state ('- [ ]' vs '- [x]', either bullet, either case) is normalized out of the material fingerprint; flipping boxes never stales an attestation — only item TEXT edits do.
2. In the AC-checkbox completeness precheck section (~L901), add one sentence: checking boxes to satisfy this precheck does not invalidate the plan-review attestation (330c normalization; single seam covers plan-review close gate and completion-verifier staleness).
3. Grep docs/ for other statements that description edits invalidate attestations (completion-verifier docs, user-guide) and align them.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [x] docs/plan-review-gate.md invalidation rules state that checkbox-state flips are normalized out of the material fingerprint and only item-text edits invalidate.
- [x] The AC-checkbox completeness precheck section notes that satisfying it is attestation-safe.
- [x] No other doc still claims box flips stale a review (grep for material-edit invalidation statements across docs/).

## File impact

- docs/plan-review-gate.md (edit)
- possibly docs/user-guide.md (edit, if it restates invalidation rules)

# J11 — Prove bidirectional reconciliation live, against a realistic store

## Why this exists

Epic e369's headline AC is:

> [operator-attested] rebar reconciles bidirectionally against the Dockerized Jira instance ... at
> least one issue created in DC appears in the local store after an inbound pass, and one local edit
> appears on the DC issue after an outbound pass, with zero unhandled exceptions

It is NOT met, and the way it failed is instructive. CI run 30637886718 reported:

    invariants: scanned=0 filed=0
    OK: steady-state pass converged
    RECON: outbound_differ total=0   inbound_differ total=0

**Scanned zero.** The pass converged because there was nothing to reconcile. That proves the reconciler runs cleanly against an EMPTY instance — it does not prove data moves. On an empty store 'converged' and 'works' are indistinguishable, and only one of them is the criterion. Closing the epic on that output would have been the fifth instance in this epic of green-but-broken.

The existing live module builds its store with the `rebar_repo` fixture: `rebar.init_repo()` on an empty temp dir. Nothing to sync, so nothing syncs.

## Approach

Run the live verification against a COPY OF THIS PROJECT'S ACTUAL TICKET STORE, so the pass sees realistic volume, ticket shapes, link graphs, comment histories and field values — the conditions that surface ordering and field-mapping defects an empty store cannot. (Deliberately NOT "pagination": that is a property of the REMOTE issue count, not of the local store, and is exercised by seeding the harness — see the volume bullet below. An earlier draft listed it here and contradicted that bullet.)

### Isolation is the first requirement, not an afterthought

rebar AUTO-COMMITS and AUTO-PUSHES ticket events to `sync.remote`. A copy of this project's store that retained its configuration could push test mutations back at the real project. Defence in depth, in priority order:

1. **A SEPARATE REPO WITH NO REMOTES — the primary mechanism.** The CI job `git init`s a fresh repo
   and copies the ticket-store content in. It never adds `origin`, so there is physically
   nowhere to push, independent of any config or env value. This is stronger than a flag
   because it cannot be defeated by a mis-read setting.
   **HOW the content is obtained, because it is NOT in a normal checkout:** `.tickets-tracker/` is
   GITIGNORED (`.gitignore:9`) and the store lives on the ORPHAN `tickets` branch, which
   `actions/checkout` does not fetch. The job must explicitly `git fetch origin tickets` in the
   SOURCE checkout and materialise that tree, then `git init` + commit it in the destination.
   Copying the workspace directory would copy nothing.
   **EXTRACT INTO `.tickets-tracker/`, NOT INTO THE REPO ROOT — an earlier draft's command was
   wrong and would have produced a store the reconciler cannot see.** The orphan `tickets` branch
   holds the ticket files AND `.bridge_state` at ITS OWN ROOT (`git ls-tree origin/tickets` shows
   `.bridge_state`, `.store-compat.json`, and bare ticket-id entries such as `003a-09ae-9983-4007`),
   whereas the reconciler reads `tracker_dir = repo_root / ".tickets-tracker"` (`reconcile.py:265`).
   Extracting to the root therefore lands every ticket one directory ABOVE where the pass looks,
   so the pass sees NO LOCAL TICKETS — a store that is empty as far as the reconciler is
   concerned, reproduced by the setup rather than by the product. (Note this does NOT surface as
   `scanned=0`: that number counts REMOTE Jira issues, not local tickets — see the store-copy AC.
   It is caught by the ticket-count check, which is why that check reads the filesystem.)
   The command is:
       mkdir -p <fresh repo>/.tickets-tracker
       git archive FETCH_HEAD | tar -x -C <fresh repo>/.tickets-tracker
   and the fixture must ASSERT the layout after extraction (ticket files exist under
   `.tickets-tracker/`) rather than trust the redirection.
   **THE WORKING REPO ALSO NEEDS A CONFIG, and it has none — it is a fresh `git init`.** The copied
   tree carries tickets, not reconciler settings, so the fixture must WRITE a `rebar.toml` into the
   fresh repo containing `[reconciler]` with `base_url = "http://localhost:2990/jira"` (plus the
   project key and `allow_insecure = true`, since the harness serves plain http). That written file is
   also what the `base_url` AC below inspects — the check and the setup must name the same file, or
   the check passes by finding nothing.
2. `REBAR_SYNC_PUSH=off` as a second, independent layer (`sync.push` accepts `always|async|off`;
   the env override is authoritative).
   **Do NOT assert on `sync.remote`.** It defaults to `"origin"` (`_config_schema.py:307`) whether or
   not such a remote exists, so "sync.remote is empty" is neither achievable nor meaningful — and
   setting it empty to satisfy a check would give false confidence while changing nothing. The
   assertion that carries real weight is that `git remote` in the working repo returns NOTHING.
3. The reconciler config points ONLY at the harness (`reconciler.base_url` = the container). No Cloud
   credentials are present in the job environment at all — no `JIRA_URL`, no `JIRA_API_TOKEN`, no
   `acli` auth — so the Cloud path cannot be driven even by accident.
4. **The isolation is ASSERTED, not assumed.** A test fails the job if `git remote` returns anything in
   the working repo. (NOT on `sync.remote` — see layer 2: it defaults to `"origin"` regardless, so
   that assertion can never pass and would only invite someone to weaken it.) Safety that is not
   tested is an intention.

### The copy must be SCRUBBED of Jira IDs and reconciler artifacts

Isolation stops ticket events ESCAPING. It does not stop the reconciler forming an intent to WRITE to a production issue key. The scrub is an independent layer and both are required.

Enumerated against this project's REAL tickets branch, not assumed:

    .bridge_state/bindings.json
    .bridge_state/bindings-retired.json
    .bridge_state/prev_snapshot.json
    .bridge_state.bak-retarget/bindings.json
    .bridge_state.bak-retarget/prev_snapshot.json

Two traps a naive scrub falls into:

* **`.bridge_state.bak-retarget/` also holds real bindings.** It is a backup left by a past project
  retarget. Deleting `.bridge_state/` by name removes the live set and leaves a SECOND full set of
  production Jira bindings in the copy. Match the pattern `.bridge_state*`, and assert none survive —
  do not delete a hardcoded list. The existence of this directory is itself proof that the artifact
  set drifts over time, so the scrub must ENUMERATE the copied tree.
* **`prev_snapshot.json` must still be scrubbed — but it is NOT detectable from mutation counts,
  and two earlier drafts of this plan got that wrong in opposite directions.** It is the OUTBOUND
  field-change baseline (`OutboundDiffConfig.prev_snapshot`, consumed in
  `outbound_differ.compute_outbound_mutations`), NOT an inbound create/delete trigger: the inbound
  and legacy differs decide creates from the CURRENT snapshot. So a leftover production copy does
  not drive mass DELETION — that much an earlier draft got right.
  What that draft then got WRONG is the claim that it produces a wave of spurious outbound UPDATEs
  that the run can detect. It cannot, and the reason is mechanical: `outbound_differ.py:518-520`
  branches on `binding_store.get_jira_key(local_id)`, and `None` routes to the CREATE path — an
  UPDATE is only ever emitted for a ticket that HAS a binding. The scrub removes `bindings.json`,
  so no ticket has one, so a `prev_snapshot.json` surviving ON ITS OWN emits nothing at all.
  **Therefore it is caught DIRECTLY, by the scrub-completeness criterion asserting `.bridge_state*`
  is absent — an observation of the file itself, not an inference from mutation counts.** See the
  zero-counts AC for the full derivation; this bullet and that AC must agree, and an earlier
  revision left them contradicting each other.

### The DC-side mutation suite

Comprehensive mutations applied to the HARNESS instance (never a real Jira), each asserted to round-trip against a NAMED per-mutation oracle (the table in the acceptance criteria gives the proving read for every cell), so the bridge is exercised rather than merely started. The ONE exception is `set_parent`'s epic case, which by design does not round-trip and is asserted directly against the transport — stated here as well as in the ACs so the two cannot drift:

* **inbound (DC -> local), fourteen mutations:** create issue; edit summary; edit description;
  transition status; add label; remove label; add comment; assign; unassign; create issue link;
  delete issue link; set sub-task parent; clear parent; delete issue (absence probe).
  **`edit comment` is deliberately NOT in this list.** An earlier draft required it in both
  directions. The reconciler has no edit-comment mutation type and `JiraDataCenterTransport` has no
  `update_comment`, so it specified a capability that does not exist. If comment editing is wanted it
  is a separate feature story, not a verification criterion.
* **outbound (local -> DC), enumerated rather than described as "the mirror set":** create ticket ->
  issue; edit title -> summary; edit description; transition status; add label; remove label; add
  comment; set assignee; clear assignee; create link; delete link; set parent; clear parent; delete
  ticket. Fourteen, matching the inbound list one-for-one — `set_parent`'s epic case is expected to
  raise `NotImplementedError` (see bda8's triage), asserted **directly against the transport**
  (`with pytest.raises(NotImplementedError): transport.set_parent(...)`), NOT through the reconciler
  subprocess. `dispatch_one._update_one_apply_parent` catches `Exception` (dispatch_one.py:564) and
  only logs, so the exception is SWALLOWED inside a pass: no traceback, unchanged return code, and
  therefore indistinguishable on the subprocess streams from a mutation that succeeded. Routing that
  assertion through the subprocess would make it untestable by construction — the same
  swallowed-exception trap that let J9's twelve missing members pass 1600 tests.
* **volume — and note WHAT drives it.** Pagination is a property of the REMOTE issue count, not of
  the local store copy. The store copy buys realistic local volume, ticket shapes and link graphs;
  it does NOT exercise paging at all. To exercise paging the suite must CREATE issues in the harness.
  Procedure, because guessing the cap is how truncation stays hidden: first READ the instance's
  effective page size (issue a `search_issues` with a high `maxResults` and observe what the server
  actually returns — Jira 8.17.1 defaults to 50, but `jira.search.views.default.max` is
  server-configurable and the server silently truncates), then seed at least `2 * observed + 1`
  issues so at least three pages are required. Assert the observed cap in the test output so a
  future instance change is visible rather than silent.
* **idempotence:** an immediately repeated pass after each direction writes nothing.

### Sequence: a thin slice BEFORE the comprehensive suite

The riskiest unknown is not any individual mutation — it is whether the copied-and-scrubbed store drives a live pass at all. So land a vertical slice first: fetch + scrub + isolation assertions, ONE inbound round-trip (create in DC, assert it appears locally) and ONE outbound round-trip (edit locally, assert it appears in DC). Only once that is green in CI does the full mutation suite go in. Building all thirteen mutations against an unproven harness path risks debugging thirteen failures that share one root cause.

## Scope

- `.github/workflows/external-integration.yml` — the `jira-dc-harness` job gains the store-copy step
  (fresh `git init`, no remote) and the isolation assertions.
- `tests/external/live_jira_dc/` — the mutation suite and its fixtures; a `dc_mutations` helper that
  applies each DC-side change through the real transport.
- `tests/external/live_jira_dc/README.md` — document the isolation contract and WHY (auto-push).

**NOT in scope:** any change that could write to this project's Jira or its tickets branch.

## Acceptance criteria

- [x] the working repo in CI has NO git remote, asserted by a test that FAILS the job otherwise —
      this is the primary isolation and it must be verified, not assumed
- [x] `REBAR_SYNC_PUSH=off` is asserted in the same test as the no-remote check
- [x] no Cloud credential is present in the job environment, asserted by test
- [x] the store under test is a COPY of this project's real ticket store, proved by COUNTING
      LOCAL TICKETS DIRECTLY — not by the pass's `scanned` number.
      **THIS AC PREVIOUSLY MEASURED THE WRONG SIDE OF THE BRIDGE, and correcting it also corrects
      this epic's founding diagnosis.** `scanned` is `len(curr_snapshot)` (`run_differs.py:282`),
      and `curr_snapshot` is `fetcher.compute_snapshot(...)` (`reconcile.py:286`) — the normalized
      **JIRA** snapshot, i.e. the count of REMOTE issues fetched from the harness. It says nothing
      whatever about how many LOCAL tickets the copied store holds. The isolated harness starts
      with no issues, so a pass run before any DC seeding reports zero no matter how large the copy
      is; the old AC would have failed on a perfectly good store, and could never have proved the
      thing it was written to prove.
      This also means the epic's original reading of the earlier failing run was wrong. That run's
      `scanned=0` was recorded (handoff #4) as "it converged because the STORE was EMPTY". On this
      code it means the HARNESS had no issues — a remote-side fact. The local store may well have
      been fine. The conclusion drawn from it (that a pass over an empty input proves nothing)
      still stands; the mechanism attributed to it does not.
      **THE CORRECT OBSERVABLE — count the copy, on the filesystem, before any pass runs.** Assert
      that the number of ticket entries under `<working repo>/.tickets-tracker/` equals the number
      on the fetched `tickets` branch (`git ls-tree --name-only FETCH_HEAD`, excluding the dot-files
      `.bridge_state*`, `.gitattributes`, `.gitignore`, `.store-compat.json`, `.ticket-write.lock`),
      and that it is > 0. Comparing the two counts rather than asserting a bare floor is what makes
      this catch a PARTIAL extraction, which a `> 0` check would wave through.
      Keep the remote-side number too, but label it honestly: after the pagination cells seed the
      harness, the same line reports how many issues the fetch actually saw, and that is the
      truncation signal the seeding criterion already owns. Where to read it, since it is not in the
      JSON envelope and two earlier revisions of this AC got the stream and the wording wrong:
      `run_differs.py:270-283` branches on
      `skip_invariant_filing = (not persist) or bool(filter_local_ids)`:
        * DRY-RUN takes the SKIP branch — `persist` is False because `MODE_CAPS[DRY_RUN] == 0`
          (`reconcile.py:218-222`) — and prints to STDERR (so no-write mode keeps STDOUT a pure
          JSON payload):
              invariants: skipped (no-write mode, <N> issues in snapshot)
          There is NO `scanned=` line in this mode at all.
        * A FILTERED pass — what the mutation cells use — hits the SAME skip branch (the gate is
          `(not persist) or bool(filter_local_ids)`) and prints
          `invariants: skipped (filtered pass, <N> issues in snapshot)` to STDERR.
        * The `scanned=<N> filed=<M> (cap=5)` line on STDOUT is emitted ONLY by an UNFILTERED
          WRITING pass — which this plan never runs (see the scoping note: unfiltered passes are
          dry-run only). It is documented here so a future reader does not go looking for that
          line in this suite's output and conclude something is broken when it is simply absent.
      Do not read `.scanned` from the envelope; there is no such key. The sibling `filed` counts
      INVARIANT-VIOLATION tickets, not tickets filed from DC issues, so `filed=0` is not evidence
      about inbound either way.
- [x] the scrub matches `.bridge_state*` as a GLOB and a test asserts ZERO binding or snapshot
      artifacts survive anywhere in the copied tree — derived by enumerating the tree, not from a
      hardcoded list
- [x] a test asserts the `.bridge_state*` scrub is COMPLETE — nothing matching `.bridge_state*`
      survives anywhere under the copied tracker dir, so a partially-scrubbed tree fails the job.
      NOT "the copied store holds no production Jira key reference", which an earlier draft required
      and which is MECHANICALLY UNACHIEVABLE: ticket event files under `.tickets-tracker/`
      legitimately embed `jira_key` values from prior Cloud syncs, the scrub correctly leaves that
      historical data intact (only BINDINGS drive remote writes — `binding_store.py:113`), so a
      whole-tree scan for production keys would ALWAYS hit and could never pass
- [x] the first pass plans EXACTLY ZERO deletion mutations AND EXACTLY ZERO outbound UPDATE
      mutations, both read from the `--mode dry-run` JSON envelope on stdout (the no-write branch at
      `__main__.py:445-452` is the one that emits JSON; writing modes emit only an `OK:` line, so
      dry-run is what makes these counts observable at all).
      **THE EXACT KEYS, so the assertion needs no guesswork.** The envelope is the whole result
      dict (`reconcile.py:690-709`). The per-mutation plan is the top-level `plan` array, built by
      `_build_plan_entries` (`reconcile_helpers.py:450-480`), whose entries are exactly
      `{direction, action, target, local_id}`. `direction` is `MutationDirection` (`"inbound"` |
      `"outbound"`) and `action` is `MutationAction` (`"create"` | `"update"` | `"delete"` |
      `"probe"` | `"clean_label"` | `"repair_property"` | `"conflict"`) — both `StrEnum`, so they
      serialize as those literal strings (`mutation.py:17-29`). The two assertions are therefore:
          jq -e '[.plan[] | select(.action == "delete")] | length == 0'
          jq -e '[.plan[] | select(.direction == "outbound" and .action == "update")] | length == 0'
      Read the envelope from STDOUT ONLY: the human-readable `OK: dry-run computed …` line goes to
      STDERR precisely so it cannot corrupt the JSON, so the test must not merge the two streams.
      **BOTH COUNTS ARE ZERO, and an earlier draft's rationale for a non-zero tolerance was
      MECHANICALLY WRONG — corrected here from the code rather than softened.** That draft said
      `< 10` outbound UPDATEs independently detects a surviving `prev_snapshot.json` while the
      deletion count stays at a reassuring zero. It cannot. `outbound_differ.py:518-520` branches
      on `binding_store.get_jira_key(local_id)`: `None` routes to the CREATE path, so an UPDATE is
      only ever emitted for a ticket that HAS a binding. The scrub removes `bindings.json`, so no
      ticket has one, so a `prev_snapshot.json` that survives on its own produces NO outbound
      updates whatsoever — the assertion it was supposed to catch that failure with is blind to it.
      What the two assertions actually do:
        * ZERO deletions catches a surviving `bindings.json` — its production keys do n … [truncated by reconciler]

content.text: ## Context
Durations profiling of the full suite (1482 tests, 16m34s). The scripts tier is ~67% of wall time; 37 of the slowest 40 are bash suites.
## Findings
Slowest: test-ticket-transition.sh 58.6s (90 write ops), test-ticket-write-commit-event.sh 44.3s, test-ticket-link.sh 32.9s (97 ops), test-ticket-lib/create/edit ~27s.

ROOT CAUSE — subprocess fan-out per operation. One rebar WRITE = cli.py python+import (~0.05s) -> bash dispatcher -> ~7 python3 heredocs (ticket-create.sh alone has 7), each a fresh interpreter, several importing the reducer -> flock + git commit. ~0.6s/write, ~0.18s/read. Suites do 25-97 ops => 15-58s. This is architectural (the bash engine), not a single bug.

REMEDY — primarily the bash->Python strangler-fig migration (epic adult-oxide-slave, Tiers A-E): collapsing per-command python3 heredocs into one in-process command removes most interpreter starts. Quick wins short of the full migration: consolidate multiple python3 heredocs within a single hot command (create/transition/link) into one python3 call; consider dropping the redundant cli.py python layer for pure bash passthroughs.

SEPARATE FINDING — reconcile retry-backoff in tests. test_mcp.py::test_reconcile_cap0_modes_allowed_in_both_gates uses _loud_acli (acli exits 99); acli-integration._call_with_backoff retries 5x with exponential backoff (2s base) => ~13.6s per test for a gate check that doesn't need a successful fetch. Quick win: use _empty_acli (fast success) for cap-0 gate tests, or cap retries via env in tests.
## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Decision recorded: which quick wins to take now vs defer to adult-oxide-slave
- [ ] cap-0 reconcile gate tests no longer pay full retry-backoff (use empty-acli or capped retries)
- [ ] Hot write commands' python3-heredoc count reduced where cheap, OR explicitly deferred to the strangler-fig tiers with a note

content.text: ## What
Introduce the low-level **bare-ref CAS lock primitive** the reconciler pass-lock and phase-gate
will sit on. Ref -> blob, so it never lives in the tickets working tree and is never union-merged.
No reconciler wiring yet (C3). Also **prove the remote feasibility** the whole design rests on.
- **AC0 feasibility spike (do this first — it gates the rest):** prove a non-branch
`refs/reconciler/*` ref pointing at a **blob** round-trips (push + fetch) through the `origin`
GitHub remote using the CI `GITHUB_TOKEN` (contents:write). If GitHub rejects it, fall back to
ref -> tiny-commit and record that in the ADR (fallback fully specified under Design decisions).
Document the working refspec.
- New module `src/rebar/_engine/rebar_reconciler/_ref_lock.py` exposing `acquire`/`release`/`read`
over a configurable ref name (`refs/reconciler/lock`, `refs/reconciler/gate` share one schema).
- **Blob = newline-terminated UTF-8 JSON** `{holder, lease_secs, heartbeat_ns, fence}`, clock from
`time.time_ns()` (NOT `rebar._store.hlc` — that fcntl cache orders ticket events, wrong tool).
`heartbeat_ns` is the acquisition/renew anchor; `fence` is a monotonic **progress-witness /
generation counter** (seeded to 0 on first acquire; C2 increments it on renew/steal) — not a full
fencing token. Decode of a corrupt/partial/empty blob **fails closed**: `read` raises a named
`RefLockCorruptError` and callers treat "cannot parse" as HELD, never free.
- **Blob creation:** `git hash-object -w --stdin` plants the blob and yields the OID, THEN
`git update-ref <ref> <oid> <old>`: **create-only CAS acquire** uses old = 40 zeros; **release
deletes the ref** (`git update-ref -d <ref> <old-oid>`) with old = the exact observed OID. A
release whose CAS sees a different oid (someone else now owns it) is a benign **idempotent success**,
not an error.
- **Reuse the real CAS helper** `_cas_advance_with_retry` (`_advisory_lock.py:447-487`), NOT a
second primitive. Its discriminator `_is_cas_mismatch` (`_advisory_lock.py:415`, hard-coding
`'refs/heads/tickets'` at line 425) is **generalized to accept the ref name** so a CAS exit-128 on
`refs/reconciler/*` is classified correctly (exact seam under Design decisions). Reuse, do not
duplicate the classifier.
- **Acquire vs release retry semantics differ** (so the reused retry loop must be told which path it
is on): a create-only **acquire** CAS exit-128 means "lock already held" — definitive, **not
retried**. A **release** CAS exit-128 (ref already gone / owned by another) is a benign **idempotent
success**, not retried. **Steal**-CAS (C2) exit-128 is the single-winner race — the loser stops and
does not re-acquire. Only genuinely transient CAS races are retried via `_cas_advance_with_retry`.
- No lease-expiry/steal logic here (that is C2); a plain `acquire` fails if the ref already exists.
- Add structured log emission for acquire-failure (already held) and release on a stale oid.
- Record the bare-ref-lock design decision (schema, CAS contract, remote refspec, operator runbook)
in a new ADR under `docs/adr/` (extended by later children).
**Why a ref lock at all (vs the workflow's `concurrency:` group in `reconcile-bridge.yml`)?**
GitHub Actions `concurrency:` only serializes runs *within one repo's workflow*; a manually-invoked
pass, a cron on a different runner, or a second clone bypasses it entirely. The ref lock is a
cross-invocation, workflow-independent guard anchored on the shared remote — the workflow group and
the ref lock are complementary, not redundant.
## Design decisions (resolves plan-review ambiguities; binding on the implementation)
1. **`_is_cas_mismatch` seam (backward-compatible).** Add an optional `ref_name: str =
"refs/heads/tickets"` parameter; the default preserves every existing call site verbatim. Thread
the ref name through the one internal use (`_advisory_lock.py:469`) and update the one external
call site (`_advisory_lock.py:585`) to pass `ref_name="refs/heads/tickets"` explicitly. No new
shared module: `_ref_lock.py` imports `_cas_advance_with_retry` / `_is_cas_mismatch` from its
sibling `_advisory_lock.py` (two call sites is below rule-of-three; C4 leaves these helpers in
place). The coupling is documented in the ADR.
2. **Three distinct exit-128 outcomes without duplicating the classifier.** Factor a
`_cas_once(...) -> bool` helper (True = CAS succeeded; False = CAS old-oid mismatch; re-raises any
non-mismatch `CalledProcessError`). `_cas_advance_with_retry` becomes `_cas_once` in the retry
loop (behaviour unchanged). `acquire` maps False -> raise `RefLockHeldError` (definitive, no
retry); `release` maps False -> return (idempotent success); C2's steal maps False -> "lost the
race", stop.
3. **`RefLockCorruptError(ValueError)`** is defined in `_ref_lock.py` and raised by `read` on any of:
empty / non-UTF-8 bytes; invalid JSON; a missing `holder`/`lease_secs`/`heartbeat_ns`/`fence`
field; `fence` not a non-negative int; `lease_secs` not a positive number. It carries the raw
bytes for debugging. Callers treat it (and any read failure) as HELD, never free.
4. **`fence` in C1.** `acquire` writes `fence=0` unconditionally (create-only CAS guarantees no prior
blob survived); `release` neither reads nor mutates `fence` (it deletes the ref). All `fence`
increment / renew / steal logic is C2.
5. **Distributed CAS via an optional `remote`.** `acquire`/`release`/`read` take an optional
`remote` argument. When `remote is None` (unit tests / local) they use a pure local
`git update-ref` CAS. When a remote is given they use the network-CAS equivalent —
`git fetch <remote> <ref>:<ref>` to sync, then `git push --force-with-lease=<ref>:<old-oid>`
(explicit lease-ref form, never bare) — which is exactly the old-oid CAS on the authoritative
remote. The reconciler passes `remote="origin"`; wiring that call and the workflow fetch refspec
are C3. AC0 proves the remote path's refspec.
6. **Subprocess timeouts.** Every `subprocess.run` in `_ref_lock.py` sets `timeout=` — 5 s for local
object/ref ops, 30 s for remote push/fetch — and a timeout raises `RefLockTimeoutError` (a
fail-closed condition; callers treat it as "cannot determine state" = HELD). Values recorded in
the ADR.
7. **AC0 ref->tiny-commit fallback (fully specified).** If GitHub rejects a blob-pointing ref, the
ref points instead at a tiny commit whose tree holds a single `lock.json` with the same schema;
`read` retrieves it via `git cat-file blob <ref>:lock.json` (commit case) vs `git cat-file blob
<ref>` (blob case), selected by `git cat-file -t <ref>`; `git hash-object -w` still plants the
payload. The CAS (create-only / observed-oid) is identical. The ADR records which path GitHub
accepted.
8. **Operator break-glass.** The ADR carries a runbook: clear a wedged lock with
`git push origin :refs/reconciler/lock` (remote) or `git update-ref -d refs/reconciler/lock`
(local). C2's lease expiry makes this rarely necessary.
## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] AC0: a proving command/test demonstrates `refs/reconciler/*` (ref -> blob) push+fetch through
the `origin` GitHub remote with the CI token; the working refspec (and the fully-specified
ref->commit fallback) is documented in the ADR.
- [ ] `src/rebar/_engine/rebar_reconciler/_ref_lock.py` provides `acquire`/`release`/`read` over a
configurable ref and an optional `remote`; acquire is create-only CAS (old=zeros), release is
observed-oid CAS; blob is created via `git hash-object -w` before `update-ref` / push.
- [ ] Blob is UTF-8 JSON `{holder, lease_secs, heartbeat_ns, fence}` (`time.time_ns()`, `fence=0` on
acquire); `read` of a corrupt/empty blob raises `RefLockCorruptError` and callers treat it as
HELD (fail-closed), never free; the corrupt conditions in Design decision 3 are each covered.
- [ ] The CAS reuses `_cas_advance_with_retry` / `_is_cas_mismatch` (`_advisory_lock.py:447-487,415`)
via the `_cas_once` seam; `_is_cas_mismatch` gains a `ref_name` param defaulting to
`refs/heads/tickets` (existing call sites unchanged); acquire exit-128 ("held") is NOT retried,
release exit-128 is idempotent success, and C2's steal exit-128 is single-winner-loss.
- [ ] Subprocess calls in `_ref_lock.py` carry timeouts (5 s local / 30 s remote) and a timeout
raises `RefLockTimeoutError` (treated as HELD).
- [ ] Structured logs are emitted for acquire-already-held and stale-oid release.
- [ ] Unit tests cover: acquire on a free ref; second concurrent acquire fails (already exists);
`read` on present vs absent ref (defined contract); release requires the correct old oid and a
stale-oid release is idempotent success; corrupt-blob decode fails closed; and a parametrized
regression that `_is_cas_mismatch` still classifies exit-128 on `refs/heads/tickets` unchanged
AND classifies exit-128 on `refs/reconciler/lock`.
- [ ] The bare-ref-lock decision (schema, CAS contract, remote refspec, fallback, timeouts, operator
runbook) is captured in a new `docs/adr/` entry. Non-integration suite green.

baseline.summary: Ref-lock primitive: bare-ref CAS acquire/release + lock-blob schema

baseline.description:
## Problem

`_PROVIDER_PREFIXES` in `src/rebar/llm/config.py` maps the `gemini` prefix to the provider name `google_genai`, but no runtime registry knows that name, so any bare `gemini-*` model id resolves to a provider that cannot be constructed and dies at call time.

Reproduced on this base (worktree at `origin/main`, `d72c477`):

    infer_provider('gemini-2.5-pro')                 -> 'google_genai'
    'google_genai' in _pydantic_ai_known_providers() -> False
    'google_genai' in KNOWN_PROVIDER_NAMES           -> False
    ProviderSession(LLMConfig())._builders           -> ['anthropic', 'bedrock']
    ProviderSession.is_resolvable('google_genai')    -> False
    ProviderSession.provider_factory('google_genai') -> LLMConfigError:
        unknown provider 'google_genai'; registered providers: ['anthropic', 'bedrock']

pydantic-ai 1.107.1 recognises `google`, `google-cloud`, `google-gla`, `google-vertex`, `vertexai` and `gateway/google-cloud`. It does NOT recognise `google_genai`.

### Which path actually breaks

There are two composition sites, and only one of them is broken — this matters for where the test goes:

- `anthropic_model._pai_model()` (used by `runner.run()` for a BARE `cfg.model`) passes the inferred
  name through a second, private table, `_PAI_PROVIDER_PREFIX`, which happens to translate
  `google_genai -> google-gla`. That path accidentally survives.
- `model_classes._resolve_target()` — the model-class / ladder path (`trivial = { model =
  "gemini-2.5-pro" }`, fallback chains, `resolve_model_string`) — uses `infer_provider`'s result
  VERBATIM and composes `google_genai:gemini-2.5-pro`. `_pai_model` then returns that string
  unchanged because it is already qualified, and provider construction raises. This is the
  end-to-end failure and is what the RED test must exercise.

The failure is at CALL time, not config time: an operator who configures a `gemini-*` model gets a plausible-looking config that fails only when a gate actually runs.

## Design decision

**Map `gemini` to `google`.** `google` is pydantic-ai's current canonical provider name for the Gemini Developer API; `google:gemini-*` ids appear directly in `known_model_names()`, and `google` is already a member of both `KNOWN_PROVIDER_NAMES` and `_pydantic_ai_known_providers()`, so `ProviderSession.is_resolvable('google')` is True and the model is left on the existing deferred lazy-string path (rebar registers no builder for it, exactly as for `openai` without a `base_url`). Building it still requires the optional `google-genai` package, and pydantic-ai's own ImportError already names the extra to install — that is the same contract every other delegate provider has, not a new failure mode.

Rejected alternatives:

- `google-gla` / `google-vertex` / `vertexai` — resolvable, but pydantic-ai 1.107.1 emits a
  deprecation warning for these prefixes and removes them in v2.0, so choosing one would
  re-introduce a scheduled break.
- Dropping the `gemini` prefix entirely so a bare `gemini-*` id fails at config time — this yields a
  WORSE outcome for an operator who has the Google extra installed: a model that pydantic-ai can
  serve today would stop being usable via a bare id.
- Adding `google_genai` to `KNOWN_PROVIDER_NAMES` (what 7b22's plan proposes for a back-compat test)
  — rejected: it makes a name that neither pydantic-ai nor rebar can build a first-class member, and
  `ProviderSession` would still refuse it. 7b22 must not lock that choice in.

`anthropic_model._PAI_PROVIDER_PREFIX` is deliberately NOT touched. Its `google_genai` key becomes unreachable from inference but is still a valid explicit-`model_provider` back-compat shim, and `capabilities.py` documents its `google-gla` output as load-bearing. Changing it is a separate concern from making the inference table agree with the registries.

## Changes

- `src/rebar/llm/config.py` — `_PROVIDER_PREFIXES`: `("gemini", "google_genai")` becomes
  `("gemini", "google")`; update the two comments that restate the old mapping (the
  `KNOWN_PROVIDER_NAMES` preamble and the `LLMConfig.model_provider` comment).
- `tests/unit/test_provider_qualifier.py` — replace `test_the_inference_path_is_not_validated`
  (which pins the defect as deliberately out of scope) with the fixed expectation; add the
  whole-table invariant and the regression pins.
- `tests/interfaces/store/test_llm_framework.py` — `test_infer_provider` pins
  `infer_provider("gemini-2.5-pro") == "google_genai"`; update to the resolvable name.

## Test plan

1. RED first, on the end-to-end mechanism: assert
   `model_classes._resolve_target("gemini-2.5-pro", None)` composes a provider string that
   `ProviderSession(LLMConfig()).is_resolvable(...)` accepts. On unfixed code this fails with
   `google_genai`.
2. AC2 invariant, parameterized over the WHOLE `_PROVIDER_PREFIXES` table (not just the gemini
   entry): every mapped provider name is in `_pydantic_ai_known_providers()` or in
   `ProviderSession._builders`, so a future added prefix cannot reintroduce the class of defect.
3. AC3 regression pins: `claude-* -> anthropic`, `gpt-*/chatgpt-* -> openai`, an already-qualified
   `google-gla:gemini-2.5-flash` still passes through unchanged, an unknown id still infers `None`.
4. Mutation-check in both directions: revert the one-line production change and confirm the new
   tests go RED; restore and confirm GREEN.
5. Gates by exit code: `make lint`, `make typecheck`, and the default `pytest` selection.

## Risk and rollback

One-line data change in a lookup table plus test updates; no control flow changes. Blast radius is limited to model ids that begin with `gemini`, which today cannot work at all. Rollback is reverting the single commit.

## Acceptance Criteria

- AC1: A bare `gemini-*` model id resolves, through both `infer_provider` and
  `model_classes._resolve_target`, to a provider name that `ProviderSession.is_resolvable` accepts.
- AC2: No value in `_PROVIDER_PREFIXES` maps to a provider name absent from both
  `_pydantic_ai_known_providers()` and `ProviderSession._builders`. A test pins this for the WHOLE
  table, not just the gemini entry, so the next added prefix cannot reintroduce the class of defect.
- AC3: Inference for `claude-*`, `gpt-*`/`chatgpt-*`, already-qualified ids, and unknown ids is
  unchanged, pinned by test.
- AC4: `make lint` and `make typecheck` pass by exit code; the default pytest selection is green.
baseline.summary: infer_provider maps gemini to google_genai, a provider neither registry knows: every bare gemini-* id is unusable

content.text: ## Finding (pre-beta deprecation sweep — meta-finding)

The `config.py:429-458` deprecation-removal registry asserts completeness ("Any alias added later MUST get a row here") but is scoped only to env/cfg/lib aliases and MISSES several genuinely-deprecated, mostly warning-emitting, user-facing surfaces. Two hygiene problems compound it: some scheduled removals emit NO runtime signal (users learn only when deleted), and the six "permanent, never-remove" ergonomic env renames nonetheless log "…is deprecated…" on every read.
Citations (registry gaps):
- MCP `list_epics` tool `src/rebar/_mcp_reads.py:239-252` (suppresses its own DeprecationWarning at :247).
- env `REBAR_LLM_MAX_ITERS` `src/rebar/llm/config.py:15,363-371` (warns via logger; lives in the LLM config layer, outside the core registry).
- CLI `--verdict-hash` `src/rebar/_commands/transition.py:45` (accepted-but-ignored; warns on stderr).
- cfg value `reconciler.lock_backend="file"` `src/rebar/_config_schema.py:335-336` (deprecated + ignored).
- Registry table `src/rebar/config.py:444-458`.

- Silent scheduled removals: `edit_ticket(tags=)` `_commands/composer.py:345-358` (no warning), flat `.rebar/config.conf` reader `config.py:303,380`, CLI `--no-sync` alias `_engine_support/reads_cli.py:624`.
- Contradiction: permanent renames warn "deprecated" `config.py:461-477`.
## Remediation
Make the registry actually complete and the signalling consistent (pre-beta hygiene; no removal here):
1. Add rows for the 4 uncatalogued deprecated surfaces (MCP list_epics, REBAR_LLM_MAX_ITERS, --verdict-hash, lock_backend="file") with horizons.

2. Ensure every scheduled-for-removal surface emits a DeprecationWarning THIS release (so beta users get a signal before v1.0.0): edit_ticket(tags=), the MCP list_epics tool (stop suppressing), the flat-conf reader, --no-sync.
3. Reconcile the "permanent rename yet warns deprecated" contradiction: either soften the wording for the six permanent env renames, or schedule them — pick one before beta.
## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] All deprecated user-facing surfaces have a registry row with a horizon (registry is genuinely complete)
- [ ] Every scheduled-removal surface emits a DeprecationWarning in this release (no silent removals at v1.0.0)
- [ ] The permanent-rename env aliases' log wording no longer claims "deprecated" (or they are scheduled) — consistent messaging
- [ ] A test/CI check asserts new aliases get a registry row

baseline.summary: Close the deprecation-registry completeness gap + fix inconsistent deprecation signalling

content.text: ## Why

S2 (urge-brook-plume) named a `merge_change_409_guard` journald event in its plan's What section for the review-bot's merge-change path. S2 implemented the guard STRUCTURALLY — a merge revision (>= 2 parents) cannot use Gerrit's bare `/patch` endpoint (it returns HTTP 409 'Revision has too many parents'), so voter.review_and_vote branches on `is_merge` BEFORE any diff fetch and routes merges through the auto-merge-delta path (`_assemble_merge_diff`) instead of `gc.get_patch` (src/rebar/review_bot/voter.py:393 vs :426; unit test asserts get_patch_calls==0 on merges). BUT the named observability event was NEVER emitted (`grep merge_change_409_guard src/` = 0 hits) — so the guard fires silently. S2's completion verifier flagged this as a valid gap; it was deferred to this follow-up.
## What

- Emit a structured `merge_change_409_guard` journald event (via the voter's `_emit`, same shape as `merge_detection`/`merge_change_review`) at the point the code enters the is_merge branch and deliberately avoids the bare `/patch` (which would 409 on a merge). Carry change_id, revision_id, parent_count.
- It fires ONLY on merges (is_merge True) — distinct from `merge_detection` (which logs is_merge for EVERY change).
- Document it in infra/runbooks/review-bot-ops.md's merge-change ops signals list.
## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] `merge_change_409_guard` structured event is emitted when the review-bot takes the merge path (is_merge, avoiding the bare /patch 409)
- [ ] The event does NOT fire on a non-merge change (guard is merge-specific)
- [ ] A unit test asserts the event fires on a merge and is absent on a non-merge (src/rebar/review_bot/voter.py path via tests/unit/test_review_bot.py)
- [ ] Documented in infra/runbooks/review-bot-ops.md merge-change ops signals

baseline.summary: Emit merge_change_409_guard event on merge-change 409 guard path (S2 follow-up)

## Why
Compaction now preserves folded event sources as `*.retired` (invariant I1, epic adept-hedge-stain / b306) instead of deleting them. Retention is currently **permanent** (accepted storage tradeoff); the tombstones accumulate on the tickets branch over time.

## What
Add a branch-wide GC sweep that removes `*.retired` files provably past **causal stability** — no clone can still be mid-reconvergence against the pre-compaction events. Must honor the concurrency doctrine (I1-I9): never remove a `.retired` whose companion `.json` could still be reintroduced by an in-flight rebase/merge.

## Scope
- A `compact-gc` (or `compact --gc`) path listing `*.retired` under the tracker, removing only those past a configurable causal-stability horizon.
- docs/concurrency.md I1: promote the 'follow-up' note to implemented behavior.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] GC removes only `*.retired` past the causal-stability horizon; recent ones kept.
- [ ] Two-clone test: a not-yet-observed compaction's `.retired` files are NOT GC'd (no resurrection window).
- [ ] fsck + replay remain clean after a GC sweep.
- [ ] docs/concurrency.md I1 updated from 'follow-up' to 'implemented'.
