baseline.description:
# Cut the overlap step's token cost: hoist the shared query digest into the cacheable system prefix

## Context / Problem

`rebar review-plan` spends the majority of its input tokens in the Stage-2 overlap judge. Measured on this repo against the real API after bug `afeb` landed (so `overlap-judge` already runs on the `standard` class, `anthropic:claude-sonnet-4-6`): 12 judge calls over a 6-candidate corpus of real `rebar.llm.enrich` digests billed **16,040 input tokens**, with `cache_read_tokens: 0` and `cache_write_tokens: 0` on every call. A recording proxy runner wrapped around the real runner in `overlap.judge.judge()` showed the query ticket's digest block present verbatim in the user message of **12 of 12** calls, while the system prompt was byte-identical across all 12. The bytes that are identical on every call are paid at full price every time, because they sit in the volatile user block, which is never a cache prefix.

## Approach

Hoist the one digest that is invariant across a batch — the query ticket's — out of the per-call user message and into the system prompt, so the shared bytes sit inside the block that already carries a cache breakpoint. The engine already applies `anthropic_cache_instructions=True` to the system block at the shared runner seam (`llm/capabilities.py:cache_settings_for`, dispatched from `llm/structured_run.py`), so no new caching machinery is added; the only reason today's calls cache nothing is that the stable block is too small. Concretely: `judge_one` gains one keyword-only argument naming which side of the pair is the hoisted digest, a module-private helper appends the digest to the system prompt, and another substitutes a fixed reference string into the slot the hoisted digest vacated.

Exact wording, so nothing load-bearing is left to the implementer's discretion. The system prompt becomes the base prompt followed by exactly:

    QUERY TICKET DIGEST — one of the two digests named below is given HERE rather than in the
    user message, because it is the same ticket in every pair of this batch. The user message
    names whether it is FIRST or SECOND for the pair at hand; read it in that position.

    <the four-line digest block produced by _digest_block>

and the reference substituted into the vacated slot is exactly `the QUERY TICKET DIGEST given in your system prompt`. That orientation paragraph also reconciles the base prompt's framing (`reviewers/overlap_judge.md`: "You are given TWO ticket digests in a fixed order"), which otherwise implies both digests arrive inline in the user message. It is appended by `judge.py` rather than edited into `overlap_judge.md`, so the prompt file keeps working unchanged for the default (non-hoisted) call shape.

`judge()` judges each candidate in BOTH orderings — `(query, cand)` and `(cand, query)` — so the query digest is FIRST in one and SECOND in the other; passing `"first"` and `"second"` respectively preserves the directional reading the prompt depends on. Because the hoisted content is the same query digest either way, the system block is byte-identical across all 2N calls of a batch: one cache write on the first call, reads on the remaining 2N-1, whenever the prefix is large enough to cache at all.

**This is NOT a byte-for-byte relocation, and it is NOT assumed to be behaviour-preserving.** The user block genuinely changes for the query side: an inline digest is replaced by a pointer to another block, which is a semantic change to a prompt whose own instructions say "false flags are costly". The engine's `resolve_prompt_cached` precedent (`llm/prompting/prompts.py:438`) is a pure stable/volatile split that does not change what the model reads, so it underwrites the SHAPE of the change but not its harmlessness. Behavioural equivalence is therefore a thing this ticket MEASURES, not a thing it asserts: a verdict-parity run over the same corpus (below) compares the per-pair `relation`, `shared_artifact` and `confidence` produced by the inline-digest baseline against the hoisted build, and a divergence is a finding to report, not a rounding error to absorb.

**Riskiest assumption, tested first — and it has already been measured, in the unfavourable direction.** The design pays off only if the hoisted prefix reaches the model's minimum cacheable prefix. `llm/capabilities.py:330` hardcodes `CACHE_MIN_PREFIX_TOKENS = 4096` and documents it as the *Opus 4.8* floor. Two probes settled what actually applies to `claude-sonnet-4-6`:

| probe | system tokens (Anthropic `count_tokens`) | call 1 write/read | call 2 write/read |
|---|---|---|---|
| bare API, `cache_control` on system | 922 | 0 / 0 | 0 / 0 |
| bare API | 1042 | 1035 / 0 | 0 / 1035 |
| through the real judge request path | 875 | 0 / 0 | 0 / 0 |
| through the real judge request path | 1250 | 1243 / 0 | 0 / 1243 |

So the real floor is **1024**, not 4096, and the caching machinery demonstrably works on this exact request path. But the hoisted prefix does not reach it: `count_tokens` over the base prompt plus each of the seven real digests gives **728–875 tokens** (base 423; digests 306–453) — every one short of 1024 by 149–296 tokens. A scratch run of the hoisted payload against the real API over the same 12 calls confirmed the consequence directly: `cache_read_tokens: 0`, `cache_write_tokens: 0`, and **16,748** input tokens versus the baseline's 16,040 — a **+708 token (+4.4%) increase**, entirely attributable to the added orientation paragraph.

**Why land it anyway, stated plainly rather than dressed up as a win.** The hoist is the structural precondition for any caching of this call site: while the shared digest sits in the user block, no floor, model change, or prompt growth can ever make it cacheable, and the cost question stays unanswerable. With the digest in the stable block the entire question collapses to one measurable number — stable-prefix tokens versus the model's floor — which this ticket pins at 728–875 vs 1024 and hands to the epic as a decided fact instead of an estimate. The residual cost is bounded and small (one orientation paragraph, ~50 tokens per call), and the criteria below require it to be reported honestly as a regression if that is what the final measurement shows. The alternative lever for closing the 149–296 token gap (batching several candidates into one call, which cuts call count AND raises the prefix past the floor) is deliberately NOT taken here — it changes the judge's precision contract and belongs on its own ticket, filed as discovered work with these measurements attached.

Deliberately NOT done here: the loop is not parallelized. `judge()` is a sequential `for cand in candidates:`, so the first call warms the prefix and the rest read it. Fanning out cold calls that share a prefix would turn one cache write plus N-1 cheap reads into N premium writes — strictly worse than today — so parallelism stays out until it can be sequenced behind a completed warm-up call.

## Scope

- `src/rebar/llm/overlap/judge.py` — the only production change: the keyword-only shared-side
  argument on `judge_one`, the two module-private helpers, and the two call sites in `judge()`.
  Omitting the argument reproduces today's exact request bytes.
- `tests/unit/test_overlap_judge.py` — the new tests below, added to the existing file.

No other file changes. `src/rebar/llm/overlap/retrieve.py` and `src/rebar/llm/overlap/wire.py` were declared while the BM25F-tightening and fail-safe options were still open; the chosen design touches neither, and both fail-safes (`wire.overlap_findings`'s `except` and `judge_one`'s `except`) are preserved unedited. `src/rebar/llm/reviewers/overlap_judge.md` is deliberately NOT edited, for the reason given above. `llm/capabilities.py`'s 4096 constant is NOT changed here: it is correct for the Opus-class model it documents, and making it model-aware is separate work filed as discovered.

## Testing

Offline tests drive the real `judge()` through a recording fake runner that captures each `RunRequest`, so they assert on the ACTUAL request payload, never on a proxy that would pass either way. The behavioural and token questions are settled by real-API runs recorded on the ticket.

- **Happy path — the shared digest is hoisted and not duplicated.** One query digest, two candidate
  digests (4 calls). Assert every captured `system_prompt` is byte-identical; the query digest block
  appears in it; the query digest block appears in ZERO of the 4 `instructions`; each candidate's
  block appears in its own `instructions`.
- **Ordered-pair semantics survive the hoist.** For the same run, assert the reference string
  occupies the FIRST slot and the candidate block the SECOND slot in ordering 1, and the reverse in
  ordering 2.
- **Failure/edge path.** A runner raising on every call still yields `judge(...) == []` with nothing
  propagating; a candidate absent from the corpus is skipped with no call made.
- **Back-compat edge.** `judge_one` without the new argument produces `system_prompt` and
  `instructions` byte-identical to today's shape.
- **Behavioural equivalence, real API.** The same query ticket and the same candidate corpus are run
  twice — once on the inline-digest baseline, once on the hoisted build — and the per-pair
  `relation`, `shared_artifact` and `confidence` are compared pair by pair.
- **Mutation check, both directions, for every new test:** revert `judge.py`, confirm each new test
  FAILS; restore, confirm it passes. Recorded on the ticket.
- Gates: `make lint`, `make typecheck`, and `pytest -m "not integration and not external" -n 6
  --dist worksteal -q`, judged by exit code.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] The query digest is sent in the system prompt and nowhere else: a recording-runner test over
      `judge()` shows it in a byte-identical `system_prompt` on every call and in ZERO
      `instructions`; checked by the new test in `tests/unit/test_overlap_judge.py`.
- [ ] Ordered-pair semantics are preserved in the payload: a test asserts the reference string is in
      the FIRST slot for ordering 1 and the SECOND slot for ordering 2, candidate block in the
      other; checked by the new ordering test.
- [ ] Judgement precision is shown, not assumed: a real-API verdict-parity run over one query ticket
      and at least six candidate digests reports, per ordered pair, the baseline vs hoisted
      `relation` / `shared_artifact` / `confidence`, and is recorded as a ticket comment. Any pair
      whose `relation` differs is called out explicitly with its digests; identical relations on
      every pair is the pass condition, and a divergence must be reported rather than averaged away.
- [ ] The step stays advisory and fail-safe: with a runner that raises on every call, `judge()`
      returns `[]` and raises nothing; checked by the extended error test.
- [ ] The default path is byte-identical: `judge_one` without the new keyword argument produces the
      same `system_prompt` and `instructions` as before; checked by the back-compat test.
- [ ] A BEFORE/AFTER measurement from real `anthropic:claude-sonnet-4-6` calls over the SAME query
      ticket and SAME corpus is recorded as a ticket comment reporting total `input_tokens`,
      `cache_read_tokens` AND `cache_write_tokens` for both runs, plus the `count_tokens` size of the
      hoisted prefix beside the measured 1024 floor. `cache_write_tokens` above one prefix write
      FAILS this criterion. A net token INCREASE is a valid outcome and must be recorded as a
      regression in plain terms, not presented as a win.
- [ ] The measured shortfall is handed on rather than dropped: a follow-up ticket is created and
      linked `discovered_from` this one, carrying the 728–875 vs 1024 numbers and naming the
      call-batching lever as the way to close the gap; checked by the linked ticket id being
      recorded in a comment here.
- [ ] Every new test is mutation-checked in both directions (fails with `judge.py` reverted, passes
      restored) and the evidence recorded as a ticket comment.
- [ ] `make lint`, `make typecheck`, and the non-integration pytest run all exit 0.
baseline.summary: Cut the overlap step's token cost: hoist the shared query digest into the cacheable system prefix

baseline.description:
## Why
The auto-lander needs an opt-in, machine-readable "please land this" intent that agents set and the bot consumes as a lease. Under Fast-Forward-Only `main` (ADR-0040) the label must be **non-gating** (FFO already enforces up-to-date, so gating would be redundant and add a wedge) and **non-sticky** (it is about the current tip). Research (GerriScary/CVE-2025-1568) requires a tight vote ACL.

> **Name collision:** `Autosubmit` must be a **project-authored label**, NOT Gerrit's first-party `autosubmit` submit-plugin (lowercase) — the plugin auto-submits on gate satisfaction, which is not what we want. Author our own label.

## What
Author an `Autosubmit` Gerrit label in `infra/gerrit/project.config` and apply it to live `refs/meta/config` (operator cutover — detect-only under ADR-0026). Vote ACL granted to **`Contributors` (requesters) AND `Administrators`** (matching the existing `LLM-Review`/`Verified` two-line pattern, so admins retain a manual set/clear fallback). Canonical ACL lines: `[access "refs/heads/*"] label-Autosubmit = -1..+1 group Contributors` **and** `label-Autosubmit = -1..+1 group Administrators`. `function = NoBlock`; empty `copyCondition`. Setting the label only REQUESTS a land (non-gating); the bot still requires `is:submittable` (both real votes MAX) and re-verifies at submit, so a requester-votable ACL is not a security vector. **This canonical account/group naming is what the epic and downstream stories reference.**

## Scope
`project.config` label block + vote ACL + the pre-cutover access snapshot + the live `refs/meta/config` cutover, PLUS a `setup-project.sh` commit-message/update touch so the cutover is reflected in the audit trail. The `Autosubmit` label block's **header comment in `project.config` is S1's own security-invariant artifact** (see AC below): it records, inline where the label is defined, why the label cannot weaken the two-vote gate. The full ADR-0042 **is authored downstream by S6 (`broken-checkered-tiger`)** — S1 does NOT create or amend ADR-0042; S1 supplies the config facts + snapshot that ADR-0042's security section later consolidates and diffs against (forward reference). The service that reads the label is a separate story (S2).

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] `Autosubmit` label added to `infra/gerrit/project.config` with `-1..+1`, `function = NoBlock`, empty `copyCondition` (drops on every new patchset), and explicit value lines: `value = 0 No score`, `value = +1 Land this change`, and `value = -1 Do not land` (the `-1..+1` range is fixed, so all three value lines are required — the `-1` line is NOT optional).
- [ ] `label-Autosubmit` vote ACL granted via **two** lines in `[access "refs/heads/*"]` — `label-Autosubmit = -1..+1 group Contributors` (requesters set it under their own identity via S4's `land`) **and** `label-Autosubmit = -1..+1 group Administrators` (manual operator fallback: set/clear a stale vote), mirroring the existing `LLM-Review`/`Verified` two-line grants. `addPatchSet` cannot forge it (empty `copyCondition` drops it on every new patchset).
- [ ] Label is NOT referenced by any submit requirement (non-gating; FFO enforces up-to-date structurally).
- [ ] **Pre-cutover access baseline captured BEFORE the label is pushed:** save the current `GET /a/projects/rebar/access` response to `infra/gerrit/access-snapshot-pre-autolander.json` and commit it in the SAME change that adds the label to `project.config`, so ADR-0042's security-invariants access-diff has a committed baseline. (Capture happens before the `refs/meta/config` push; the label add and the snapshot commit ship together.)
- [ ] `config-check` passes; live cutover applied to `refs/meta/config` and verified via `GET /a/projects/rebar/labels/Autosubmit`; a post-cutover `GET /a/projects/rebar/access` diffs cleanly against `infra/gerrit/access-snapshot-pre-autolander.json` showing ONLY the added `label-Autosubmit` vote grants (no other ACL drift).
- [ ] **Security-invariants artifact (S1's own deliverable — an inline header comment, NOT the downstream ADR):** the `[label "Autosubmit"]` block in `infra/gerrit/project.config` carries a header comment recording the "non-gating label + bot re-verifies the two-vote gate on the exact tested SHA at submit" invariant (the protection is the re-verify at submit, NOT restricting who may set `Autosubmit`) with its concrete checks — a `grep` of `infra/gerrit/project.config` proving `function = NoBlock` and no submit-requirement reference, and the note that the bot only submits when `is:submittable` holds on the tested SHA — demonstrating the label cannot weaken the two-vote (`LLM-Review`+`Verified`) gate. The header comment also notes the **name collision** (this is a project-authored `Autosubmit` label, NOT Gerrit's first-party `autosubmit` submit-plugin, which we deliberately do not use). **S6's ADR-0042 later consolidates this invariant (forward reference); S1 does not author ADR-0042.**
- [ ] **`setup-project.sh` reflects the cutover:** `infra/gerrit/setup-project.sh` is updated so its `refs/meta/config` push commit message names the `Autosubmit` label + ACL addition (audit trail). **Proving command:** `grep -F 'Autosubmit' infra/gerrit/setup-project.sh` returns a match.
baseline.summary: S1 Autosubmit label + ACLs (project.config + refs/meta/config cutover)

content.text: ## Why
Epic `850f`'s seam (S2) is inert until a real backend plugs in. This story adds the v1 T2 backend —
one-shot `pyright --outputjson` diagnostics for Python — behind S2's `refute_semantic` dispatch,
turning the abstain-by-default seam into a working confirm-only semantic resolver. It is self-contained
and opt-in: gated behind an optional extra plus `t2_enabled`, and it abstains (never raises) when
pyright is absent.
## What
- New module `src/rebar/grounding/pyright_backend.py`:
- A `refute(reference, *, repo_root, timeout, cache=None) -> dict` that `semantic.refute_semantic`
dispatches to when `t2_backend == "pyright"`. Runs `pyright --outputjson` over the **project root**
(not single-file, so cross-module imports resolve) via the fail-open `harness.run_tool` with the
configured timeout; caches the parsed result in the caller-owned `cache` keyed by project root
(one invocation per review, reused across references).
- **Confirm-only mapping** for a reference in file `in_file`:
- `refuted@T2` iff pyright ran and produced parseable JSON, AND `in_file` has **zero**
import-resolution diagnostics (`reportMissingImports` / `reportMissingModuleSource` = env built),
AND no diagnostic in `in_file` "concerns the reference" (an unresolved-kind rule —
`reportAttributeAccessIssue` / `reportUndefinedVariable` / unresolved-import — whose message
names the reference's leaf `name`). Since `validate_reference` carries no line/span, matching is
by file + rule-kind + the leaf name appearing in the diagnostic message.
- `abstain@T2` (closed reason) otherwise: `no_tool` (pyright absent), `unsupported_lang`
(reference language is not Python), `ambiguous` (no `in_file` to locate), `parse_error`
(unparseable output), `timeout`, `other` (crash / env-not-built / a diagnostic sits at the
reference — a suspected-absent is never asserted). Any diagnostic rule the mapping does not
recognize routes to `abstain`, never `refuted` (fail-safe).
- A `version() -> str | None` PATH/`--version` probe (fail-open) and registration into
`semantic.T2_BACKENDS` + `available_backends()`.
- Add the optional extra `grounding-t2 = ["pyright>=1.1"]` to `pyproject.toml`; guard the pyright
invocation so a non-adopting client (extra not installed / pyright not on PATH) pays nothing and gets
`abstain(no_tool)`.
- Docs: a T2 section in `docs/grounding.md` describing the backend, the confirm-only mapping, the three
`.rebar/grounding.toml` keys, and the `grounding-t2` extra.
- Tests: `tests/unit/grounding/test_pyright_backend.py` — a fail-open matrix pinned against captured
real `pyright --outputjson` fixtures.
## Scope
In scope: `pyright_backend.py`, the `grounding-t2` extra, `docs/grounding.md` T2 section, fixtures +
tests, and registering the backend into S2's `T2_BACKENDS`. Depends on S2's seam. Out of scope:
additional languages/backends (future work behind the same seam).
## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] `src/rebar/grounding/pyright_backend.py` implements `refute`, `version`, and registers `"pyright"`
into `semantic.T2_BACKENDS` and `available_backends()`.
- [ ] With `t2_enabled=true, t2_backend="pyright"`, a member/dotted reference that resolves in a Python
fixture whose imports all resolve yields `refuted` at `TIER_T2`.
- [ ] The same reference with an unresolved attribute (imports otherwise resolving) yields `abstain` at
`TIER_T2` (never an asserted absence).
- [ ] Fail-open matrix, each mapping to `abstain` with the stated closed reason: pyright off `PATH`
→ `no_tool`; non-Python reference → `unsupported_lang`; reference with no `in_file` → `ambiguous`;
unparseable pyright output → `parse_error`; simulated timeout → `timeout`; a file with
`reportMissingImports` (env-not-built) → `other`; a subprocess crash → `other`.
- [ ] A test asserts `refute` returns only `refuted` or `abstain` outcomes across the whole matrix
(the confirm-only guarantee).
- [ ] `pyproject.toml` declares the `grounding-t2` extra.
- [ ] A test with pyright removed from `PATH` shows the backend returns `abstain(no_tool)` without
raising.
- [ ] `grounding_info()` lists the pyright backend with its detected availability/version.
- [ ] `grounding_info()` output validates against `grounding_info.schema.json` after the change.
- [ ] `docs/grounding.md` has a T2 section documenting the backend, the mapping, the config keys, and
the extra.
- [ ] `pytest tests/unit/grounding/` exits 0.
- [ ] `make lint` exits 0.

baseline.summary: T2 grounding S3: pyright --outputjson diagnostics backend + grounding-t2 extra + fail-open matrix

# A failed LLM call is invisible in `$REBAR_USAGE_LOG`

## Reported by

`rebar review-code` on change 1178 (story b690), as a medium/correctness advisory finding against that change. **Verified and confirmed PRE-EXISTING, not introduced by b690** — b690 only added `step`/`model_class` fields to rows that are written; the omission of failed calls predates it.

## Mechanism (verified by reading the control flow, not inferred)

`PydanticAIRunner.run()` calls `usage_log.record(...)` at the END of the method, AFTER the `try/except` whose except spine is `interpret_failure(exc, ...)`, and `interpret_failure` ALWAYS re-raises. So when a model call raises — budget exceeded, provider error, unretryable output, sampling error — control leaves `run()` without ever reaching `record()`, and NO usage row is written for a call that may have burned substantial input tokens.

## What this does and does not cost

**Failure spend is not lost entirely.** `usage_log.failure_usage()` builds safe counters (requests, tool_calls, the four token fields, finish_reason) and `structured_run.py` attaches them as `exc.diagnostic` at four sites (`:91`, `:100`, `:119`, `:134`), which reach the durable gate-error sidecar. So the information exists.

**But it never reaches the usage log**, which means:
- a spend total folded from the JSONL by `summarize()` UNDER-REPORTS actual spend, silently, by
  exactly the failed calls. That summary is what the two billable weekly CI jobs
  (`external-integration.yml`, `prompt-eval.yml`) publish to `$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY`.
- the per-step attribution added by b690 cannot see failed calls, so "which pass is expensive?"
  is answerable only for calls that succeeded — and a retry-to-exhaustion failure is precisely the
  expensive case an operator would want attributed.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] a failed LLM call writes a usage row carrying the same identifying fields a successful one
      does (`op`, `step`, `model_class`, `model`, `provider`) plus whatever token counters are
      known, so a JSONL spend total includes failed calls
- [ ] the row is distinguishable from a successful call (so a reader can separate delivered work
      from burned budget) — the shape is the implementer's call, but it must be explicit, not
      inferred from a missing field
- [ ] asserted by a test in which the model RAISES and the log is then read — not by reading
      `usage_log.py`, and not by asserting on `failure_usage()` in isolation, since the defect is
      about what reaches the FILE
- [ ] the existing no-op-when-unset and `summarize()`-still-folds guarantees still hold
- [ ] telemetry must never break the call path: the record must not convert a provider failure into
      a different exception, nor swallow the original (the existing `record()` already swallows its
      own OSError for this reason — preserve that discipline)
- [ ] no double-counting: a call that fails and is then RETRIED must not be recorded such that the
      same spend appears twice as delivered work

## Note on scope

Not fixed inside b690 deliberately: b690's change is a one-line model-resolution fix plus its observability prerequisite, and moving `record()` across an exception boundary is a distinct behavioural change to the failure path with its own double-counting and never-break-the-call-path risks. Filed under epic 061c because the usage log is that epic's measurement instrument.
baseline.summary: Usage log omits failed LLM calls: record() sits after run()'s except spine, so a raising call writes no row

# The bugfix-size attestation gate is unsatisfiable for any locally-reviewed bug

## Context / Problem

`bugfix_size_gate.py` (landed on main 2026-08-03, commit 1920dc9fe5) BLOCKS a Gerrit change whose `rebar-ticket:` bug carries >150 non-test changed lines unless that bug has an acceptable plan-review attestation. Its "cross-host verification" design constraint is explicit:

    the review bot is NOT the environment that signed the attestation, so this module verifies
    the op-cert against the PINNED `.rebar/trusted_environments.yaml` keyring (never the bot's
    own env key), mirroring `verify_required_environment`'s not-pinned arm for unpinned
    principals.

`.rebar/trusted_environments.yaml` on main pins exactly ONE environment: `9f1c8e42-7a3b-4d5e-b6c1-2f0a9d8e7c65` (`nava-opcert-prod`), whose private half "lives ONLY in SSM /rebar/prod/opcert-ed25519-key".

A plan review run by a developer signs with that developer's own env id as the DSSE principal. That principal is not pinned, so `trusted_env_keyring(principal, repo_root)` returns None and the gate takes its not-pinned arm:

    {"verdict": "mismatch",
     "reason": "signing environment '<env>' is not pinned in trusted_environments.yaml"}

which is an affirmative invalid classification, so it BLOCKS (it is not one of the fail-open infrastructure arms, and it is not one of the ACCEPTED `stale-code`/`stale-head` drift arms).

**So a large bug fix can only clear this gate with an attestation produced by the prod op-cert environment — and there is no way to obtain one.** The deployed `opcert` service does accept `{"ticket_id", "kind": "plan-review"}` on `POST /opcert/jobs` and signs with the SSM key, but:

1. **no client exists in the repo.** `grep` for `opcert/jobs` outside `opcert_service/app.py`
   finds only the nginx template, the terraform output description, and unit tests. Callers are
   expected to SigV4-sign to an API Gateway endpoint; nothing in `rebar` does.
2. **the service deliberately cannot persist what it signs.** compose sets
   `REBAR_SYNC_PUSH: "off"` with the comment "a gate's SIGNATURE append lands only in the
   discarded per-job workspace". It returns the `envelope` in the job record, and there is no
   rebar CLI that records a returned envelope onto a ticket as its attestation.
3. **the guard is a production secret.** `/opcert/jobs` fails closed without the
   `X-Opcert-Guard` header, materialized from SSM `/rebar/prod/opcert-origin-guard`.

## Evidence this is live, not theoretical

Gerrit change 1344 (bug `129e-2d88-cce2-492c`, 554 non-test lines) is **`Verified +1`** with its only blocking finding being this criterion. Its plan review PASSED and was re-signed locally; the gate's complaint moved from "unsigned; no plan-review attestation record" (patchset 1) to "mismatch; signing environment 'ade0f2ef-…' is not pinned" (patchset 2), i.e. the signature IS seen and is rejected solely on provenance. No code finding blocks the change.

`129e` in turn `blocks` epic `061c-ecd1-8967-4a76`, so this gate currently blocks an epic.

## Why no existing bug fix hit this first

The gate landed 2026-08-03. The only recent bug fix over the floor, `e3cd-ba36-41c3-4661` (229 non-test lines), merged 2026-08-02 — ONE DAY BEFORE the gate existed — and carries no attestation at all (`review-plan --status` -> "unsigned"). So there is no precedent path; 129e appears to be the first change to actually meet this gate.

## Scope

- `src/rebar/llm/code_review/bugfix_size_gate.py` — the not-pinned arm's severity/classification.
- `.rebar/trusted_environments.yaml` — whether developer signing environments are pinnable at all.
- a missing client for the op-cert service (submit + record the returned envelope), if the
  intended answer is that large bug fixes must be prod-attested.
- `docs/plan-review-gate.md` / the packaged code-review guide — neither tells an author how to
  obtain an acceptable attestation for a large fix.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] a large bug fix authored in a developer environment has a DOCUMENTED, EXECUTABLE path to an
      attestation this gate accepts — demonstrated end to end on a real change, not by inspection
- [ ] the not-pinned arm's behaviour is a deliberate, recorded decision: either it stays blocking
      and the path above exists, or it is reclassified (e.g. advisory when NO developer environment
      is pinnable), with the security reasoning written down
- [ ] the failure message names the remedy, so an author hitting it is not left to reverse-engineer
      trusted_environments.yaml and the compose file to discover why a PASSING plan review is
      rejected
- [ ] whatever path is chosen does NOT let a change self-certify from an untrusted environment —
      the gate's original intent (no drive-by rewrite labeled as a fix) is preserved
baseline.summary: bugfix-size attestation gate is unsatisfiable for any locally-reviewed bug — only the prod op-cert env is pinned and it has no client

## Context / Problem

The `commit-msg` hook install command documented in AGENTS.md and CONTRIBUTING.md is WORKTREE-UNSAFE. It silently clobbers the shared, pre-commit-managed hook for EVERY worktree, and the damage is invisible until a Gerrit push is rejected for a missing `Change-Id`.

The documented command:

    curl -sLo "$(git rev-parse --git-path hooks/commit-msg)" https://rebar.solutions.navateam.com/tools/hooks/commit-msg && chmod +x "$(git rev-parse --git-path hooks/commit-msg)"

`git rev-parse --git-path hooks/commit-msg` run from inside a linked worktree does NOT resolve to that worktree — hooks live in the shared common dir, so it resolves to `/…/rebar/.git/hooks/commit-msg`. The curl therefore OVERWRITES the pre-commit wrapper in the main checkout.

## Why the damage is worse than one broken worktree

`.pre-commit-config.yaml:16-19` documents the intended arrangement explicitly: pre-commit installs in MIGRATION mode, preserving Gerrit's hook as `commit-msg.legacy` and running BOTH, and warns "never install with `-f`/`--overwrite`, which would drop the Change-Id stamp and break every push to Gerrit." The curl achieves exactly that forbidden state by a different route — it replaces the wrapper rather than chaining to it, so the pre-commit `commit-msg` gate (the 50/72 message rule) stops running, and once someone later reinstalls pre-commit over it the Gerrit stamper is the half that disappears.

Either way the failure is SILENT at commit time and only surfaces at `git push gerrit`, potentially many commits later, in a DIFFERENT worktree than the one that ran the curl.

## Evidence: this is not hypothetical, it happened twice in one session

Two independent agents, working different tickets in different worktrees, each ran the documented command and each clobbered `/Users/joeoakhart/rebar/.git/hooks/commit-msg`. Both noticed and repaired it with `make hooks`, and the repaired state was verified both times:

    commit-msg          641 bytes   pre-commit wrapper
    commit-msg.legacy  3127 bytes   Gerrit stamper, contains the Change-Id logic

They noticed because they were told to report side effects. An agent not told to look would have left the repo with Change-Id stamping broken for every worktree on the host.

## Approach

Make the documented command worktree-correct and non-destructive. Options to weigh, not yet decided:

- Resolve the shared hooks dir deliberately and refuse to overwrite a pre-commit wrapper, instructing
  the user to run `make hooks` instead.
- Fold the Gerrit hook install into `make hooks` so there is ONE documented way to get both hooks and
  it is idempotent — this is the likely right answer, since `make hooks` already owns the chained
  arrangement.
- Have the command write `commit-msg.legacy` directly when a pre-commit wrapper is present.

Whichever is chosen, the docs in AGENTS.md and CONTRIBUTING.md must stop telling contributors to curl over `--git-path hooks/commit-msg`.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [x] Running the documented install from inside a linked worktree leaves BOTH hooks functional: the
      pre-commit wrapper and the Gerrit Change-Id stamper.
- [x] A test or scripted check asserts that after the documented install, a commit made in a worktree
      receives a `Change-Id` AND is subject to the pre-commit `commit-msg` gate.
- [x] AGENTS.md and CONTRIBUTING.md no longer instruct a bare curl over
      `$(git rev-parse --git-path hooks/commit-msg)`.
- [x] The failure mode is made loud rather than silent: attempting the unsafe overwrite warns or
      refuses instead of succeeding quietly.
- [x] make lint and make typecheck pass by exit code; the default selection is green.
baseline.summary: The documented commit-msg hook install is worktree-unsafe and silently clobbers Change-Id stamping for every worktree

# B — Project-only coaching move: direct the agent to Serena when source references are missed

## Context / Problem

A reminder at grep-time (story A) is preventive. This story adds the **corrective** half: when a review actually finds that source-code references were enumerated by hand or incompletely, the agent should be coached to re-derive them with Serena. This is the same failure that produced three under-enumerated Scope sections in epic `061c` (the epic itself, S1 naming two of three patch sites, S2 naming two of four affected test files).

## Verified ground truth (probed 2026-07-29; resolves the plan's "known unknown")

The original plan left "are code-review coaching moves overlay-driven?" open and made scope contingent on it. It is resolved, and the answer changes the routing decision:

1. **Code-review moves ARE already overlay-driven.** `src/rebar/llm/code_review/moves.py::load_move_registry`
   (lines 86-103) merges project extensions from **`.rebar/code_review_moves.json`** — a *different* file from
   `.rebar/plan_review_moves.json`. So **no engine wiring is needed**, and the contingent
   `src/rebar/llm/...` scope item is dropped.
2. **But a `project.*` criterion id can never fire a code-review move.** Code-review `applies_when` tags are
   drawn from the **closed** `{OVERLAY_IDS ∪ "always"}` vocabulary (`code_review/moves.py:1-9`, 58-60), and the
   gate's `active_triggers` is the union of the surviving findings' *overlay* `criteria`
   (`code_review/workflow_ops.py::code_review_coach_inputs`). A move keyed
   `applies_when: ["project.symbol-reference-completeness"]` would register and then never be offered — a
   permanently dead move.
3. **Plan-review has no such restriction.** `plan_review/passes.py:765` builds `triggers` as the union of
   `criteria` carried by blocking + surviving findings, which *does* include project criterion ids — the
   existing `project.portability` / `project-portability` pair proves the path end-to-end.

**Decision, therefore: route the criterion to `plan_review` only.** That also matches the concern's own shape — "the file/symbol inventory in this plan was enumerated by hand and is incomplete" is a plan-review judgement.

## Approach

Follow the existing `project.portability` pattern exactly, which is three files:

- `.rebar/criteria_routing.json` — a new criterion `project.symbol-reference-completeness` under `plan_review`,
  with `default_posture: "advisory"` (and NO `blocking_enabled` — that field is a code-review-only
  convention which plan-review's `threshold_for` never reads (`src/rebar/llm/criteria/model.py:73-76`), so
  including it would be inert and misleading; `project.portability` carries no such field), plus its `activate`
  entry `["plan_review"]`.
- `.rebar/prompts/plan-review-project-symbol-reference-completeness.md` — the criterion's reviewer prompt:
  detect a plan whose affected-file / call-site inventory was enumerated by hand (or is demonstrably
  incomplete) rather than derived from the symbol graph.
- `.rebar/plan_review_moves.json` — the matching move `applies_when: ["project.symbol-reference-completeness"]`,
  whose template directs re-derivation with `find_referencing_symbols` **and** the string-literal sweep
  (`monkeypatch.setattr` / `getattr` / `importlib`) the LSP cannot resolve, so the coaching is complete rather
  than half-right.

**Posture: advisory, never blocking.** This coaches a method, not a correctness property; blocking on "how did you find these references" would gate process and fire noisily.

## Scope

- `.rebar/criteria_routing.json` — the new `project.*` criterion + its `activate` entry (plan_review only).
- `.rebar/prompts/plan-review-project-symbol-reference-completeness.md` — the criterion prompt.
- `.rebar/plan_review_moves.json` — the matching move.
- No `src/rebar/` change: the overlay machinery already exists (ground truth 1), so shipped defaults for other
  clients are untouched by construction.

## Testing

- A test asserts the overlay files are valid and self-consistent: the criterion id appears under `plan_review`,
  its `activate` list is exactly `["plan_review"]`, its posture is `default_posture: "advisory"` with no
  inert `blocking_enabled` key, a
  prompt file exists at the conventional path, and the move's `applies_when` names the criterion id (a move
  keyed on an id no criterion emits is dead — the failure mode ground truth 2 identified).
- A test asserts the criterion id appears nowhere under `src/rebar/` (shipped defaults unchanged for other
  clients).
- **Real run:** a `rebar review-plan` against a ticket whose inventory was hand-enumerated emits the move; the
  output is attached to this ticket as a comment.
- **Contrast:** a review of a ticket with a symbol-derived inventory does not emit it (recorded, not asserted in
  a unit test — LLM output is not deterministic enough to gate CI on).

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] a project-only criterion + coaching move exists whose move text directs re-deriving source references with
      Serena's symbol tools, INCLUDING the string-literal (`monkeypatch.setattr`/`getattr`) sweep the LSP cannot do
- [ ] the criterion is advisory via `default_posture: "advisory"` — the only field plan-review's
      `threshold_for` reads — and carries NO `blocking_enabled` key (code-review-only, inert here)
- [ ] the criterion routes to `plan_review` only, and the ticket records WHY not `code_review` (a `project.*` id
      can never enter code-review's closed `applies_when` vocabulary, so such a move would be dead)
- [ ] it is recorded on the ticket that code-review coaching moves were ALREADY overlay-driven
      (`code_review/moves.py::load_move_registry` reads `.rebar/code_review_moves.json`), so no wiring was added
- [ ] a REAL `rebar review-plan` run demonstrates the criterion, with the run log committed to
      `docs/serena-symbol-reference-coaching-sample.md` and summarised on this ticket. **AC amended by operator
      decision after 7 real runs** (see the run log): the original wording required a run whose output CONTAINS
      the coaching move, which is not achievable through the overlay. The overlay controls move
      APPLICABILITY (proven deterministically); the coach LLM controls SELECTION, and the same
      incomplete-inventory evidence also fires the BLOCKING built-ins `G1G2`/`G6`/`E4`, which Pass-4 coaches
      first, so an advisory move always loses selection — while a complete inventory makes the criterion
      correctly abstain. What is therefore required and met: (i) the criterion FIRES on a real hand-enumerated
      plan, at validity 1.0, naming the string-literal site the LSP cannot resolve; (ii) the move is proven
      APPLICABLE for its trigger set and silent otherwise; (iii) the selection limitation is documented rather
      than presented as met
- [ ] the criterion rides the `.rebar/` overlay only: a test proves the criterion id appears nowhere under
      `src/rebar/`, so the shipped default criteria set is unchanged for other rebar clients
- [ ] the contrast case is recorded: a review of a ticket with a symbol-derived inventory does not emit the move
- [ ] `make lint`, `make typecheck` and `make test` pass
baseline.summary: B — Project-only coaching move directing Serena when source references are missed

baseline.description:
## Context

Fills the **T2 semantic-resolution tier** deferred out of the code-grounding v1 floor (epic
`8f6c-6008-33f3-4f82`, closed). v1 shipped the deterministic, polyglot, fail-open **T0
(manifest/registry existence) + T1 (ctags/tree-sitter syntactic)** floor plus a **T2
abstain-by-default seam**: `TIER_T2` exists in the closed tier vocabulary but is never emitted, and
member/dotted references abstain inline in `resolve.refute_absence` (tagged "member binding is T2").
This epic wires a real, self-contained, opt-in T2 backend behind that seam **without changing the
three-valued evidence contract (`refuted` / `match` / `abstain`) or its consumers**.

Constraints any T2 backend must respect (why T2 was deferred):
- **Not deterministic by nature.** Semantic resolution is a function of machine state (installed deps,
  build state, runtime versions), not just the artifact. Every failure mode
  (not-installed / not-built / wrong-version / hung) is indistinguishable from a genuinely fake symbol.
- **Confirm-only verdict asymmetry.** A T2 `refuted` (an asserted absence disproved — the reference
  resolves) is trustworthy; an asserted absence is suspect unless the environment is known-good. So
  T2 emits a trustworthy `refuted` and otherwise **`abstain`s** (the canonical outcome for
  "unknown") — it never sits on a deterministic blocking path.
- **Cannot be borrowed from the ambient environment.** No reliance on an externally-configured MCP
  server (e.g. Serena) or a host toolchain; the backend is self-contained + opt-in.

> **Terminology (locked to the code vocabulary).** The three-valued outcome is
> `OUTCOME_REFUTED="refuted"` / `OUTCOME_MATCH="match"` / `OUTCOME_ABSTAIN="abstain"` (`evidence.py`).
> "present" is the informal gloss for `refuted` (absence disproved); "unknown" is the informal gloss
> for `abstain`. This epic writes `refuted` / `abstain` everywhere; the glosses appear only in prose.

## Decided v1 design

**Selected v1 backend: one-shot compiler/checker-CLI diagnostics** (candidate 2), starting with
`pyright --outputjson` for Python. Rationale over the alternatives: no long-lived server (simplest to
fail-open + batch), no ambient dependency (the checker is an opt-in extra / PATH probe), and it yields
a trustworthy `refuted` when the checker runs cleanly. The **bundled LSP-client library** (candidate
1) and **containerized/hermetic** (candidate 3) tiers are **deferred** — the LSP path multiplies the
per-language server/runtime/config surface; the containerized path's gating cost is an egress-locked
single-tenant microVM sandbox (arbitrary-code-execution on untrusted client repos). Both remain future
backends behind the same seam this epic establishes.

## Design specifics (resolving the plan-review indeterminates)

**The seam is a dispatch function, not a plugin registry (Rule-of-Three).** With one concrete backend
shipping, a general `T2Backend` Protocol + registry is speculative abstraction. S2 instead adds one
module `src/rebar/grounding/semantic.py` exposing:

```python
def refute_semantic(reference, *, repo_root, config, timeout=None) -> dict | None
def available_backends() -> list[dict]   # [{name, available, version}] for grounding_info, fail-open
T2_BACKENDS: tuple[str, ...] = ("pyright",)   # the closed set of selectable backend names
```

`refute_semantic` returns a **normalized T2 evidence record** (`refuted@T2` or `abstain@T2`) or
**`None`** meaning "T2 declined to run — fall back to the caller's T1 record" (default-off path). A
future backend adds a name to `T2_BACKENDS` and a branch in `refute_semantic` — no premature Protocol.

**Escalation call-site (single owner): `oracle.refute_absence`.** After the T1/deps lanes return,
if the record is an `abstain` on a `member`/dotted reference or a not-found bare `symbol`/`import`,
`oracle.refute_absence` calls `semantic.refute_semantic(...)`; a returned `refuted@T2` replaces the
T1 abstain, otherwise the T1 record is returned unchanged. `resolve.refute_absence` (the standalone
T1 lane) is **not** modified — keeping T2 out of the T1 lane preserves T1's determinism.

**Config schema** (`.rebar/grounding.toml`, `[grounding]`, read by `resolve.load_config`; default-off):
- `t2_enabled` : bool, default `false` — the master opt-in.
- `t2_backend` : string in `T2_BACKENDS`, default `"pyright"` — an unknown value fails open to
  disabled (abstain), never a raise.
- `t2_timeout_seconds` : number, default `30` — the bounded per-invocation subprocess timeout.

**`grounding_info` change is explicit code, not free.** `oracle._backend_availability()` is a
hardcoded list today; S2 appends `*semantic.available_backends()` to it. The `grounding_info` schema's
`backends[]` name field is an open string, so a new backend name validates without a schema change
(S2 adds a conformance assertion proving this).

**pyright invocation model (the trustworthiness crux).** pyright is invoked **over the project root**
(not single-file) via the fail-open `harness.run_tool` with `t2_timeout_seconds`, so cross-module
imports resolve. The confirm-only decision for a reference in file F:
- **`refuted@T2`** iff: pyright ran and produced parseable JSON, **AND** F has **zero**
  import-resolution diagnostics (`reportMissingImports` / `reportMissingModuleSource` — the
  "environment built" precondition), **AND** there is **no** diagnostic at the reference's
  span/name (`reportAttributeAccessIssue` / `reportUndefinedVariable` / unresolved-import).
- **`abstain@T2`** (closed reason) in every other case: tool absent (`no_tool`), non-Python
  reference (`unsupported_lang`), no locatable file (`ambiguous`), unparseable output
  (`parse_error`), timeout (`timeout`), crash (`other`), F has unresolved imports so the env is
  not-built (`other`, detail records it), or a diagnostic sits at the reference (`other` — a
  suspected-absent is never asserted). One pyright run per review is cached by project root and
  reused across references (no per-reference re-invocation).

If real pyright output does not cleanly partition these diagnostic codes, the backend **abstains**
(fail-safe): S3's tests pin the mapping against captured real `--outputjson` fixtures, and any
unmapped/ambiguous code routes to `abstain`, never `refuted`.

## Related: IaC grounding lane — split out

The Terraform `validate`/Registry/`plan` tiering is a distinct domain (not a code-build environment)
— it becomes its **own sibling epic** (created by S1, linked `relates_to`), not a child here.

## Decomposition (3 stacked children, bottom → top; landed as one Gerrit feature branch)

- **S1 — ADR + IaC split (design/doc):** an ADR under `docs/adr/` recording the backend selection,
  the confirm-only mapping, the minimal-seam (no-registry) decision, and the deferral of
  LSP-lib/containerized; plus creation of the sibling IaC epic.
- **S2 — T2 seam (default-off):** `semantic.py` (`refute_semantic` / `available_backends` /
  `T2_BACKENDS`), the three config keys, escalation in `oracle.refute_absence`, and
  `_backend_availability()` reporting — all default-off so behavior is byte-identical when
  `t2_enabled=false`, proven by a regression test.
- **S3 — pyright diagnostics backend:** the Python backend `refute_semantic` dispatches to, the
  optional `grounding-t2` extra, docs (`docs/grounding.md` T2 section + config keys), and a
  per-backend fail-open matrix pinned against real pyright `--outputjson` fixtures.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] S1 lands an ADR under `docs/adr/` that names the v1 backend (pyright compiler-CLI diagnostics),
      records the confirm-only mapping and the minimal-seam decision, and creates + links a sibling
      IaC epic; the LSP-lib and containerized tiers are recorded as deferred with their tradeoffs.
- [ ] S2 lands `semantic.refute_semantic`/`available_backends`/`T2_BACKENDS`, the three
      `.rebar/grounding.toml` keys, the `oracle.refute_absence` escalation, and the
      `_backend_availability()` reporting — with `t2_enabled=false` producing byte-identical evidence
      to pre-epic behavior, proven by a default-off regression test in `tests/unit/grounding/`.
- [ ] S3 lands the pyright backend that emits `refuted@T2` when pyright runs, the file has zero
      import-resolution diagnostics, and there is no diagnostic at the reference; and emits
      `abstain@T2` with a closed reason for tool-absent / non-Python / no-file / parse-error /
      timeout / crash / env-not-built / diagnostic-at-reference.
- [ ] No code path emits an asserted absence: verified by a test asserting `refute_semantic` returns
      only `refuted` or `abstain` outcomes across the fail-open matrix.
- [ ] Self-contained + opt-in: the backend is gated behind the `grounding-t2` optional extra plus
      `t2_enabled`, and returns `abstain(no_tool)` (never a raise) when pyright is absent — proven by
      a test that runs with pyright off `PATH`.
- [ ] Fail-open matrix passes for the pyright backend (unsupported lang / no tool / no locatable file
      / crash / timeout / diagnostic-present / env-not-built → `abstain`), pinned against captured
      real `pyright --outputjson` fixtures.
- [ ] `grounding_info` (CLI `grounding-info`, MCP `grounding_info`, library `rebar.grounding_info()`)
      lists the pyright T2 backend with its detected availability/version, and the output still
      validates against `grounding_info.schema.json`.
- [ ] Proving command green: `pytest tests/unit/grounding/ && make lint` passes; all three children
      (S1–S3) closed and landed on `main` via the Gerrit feature branch.
- [ ] One self-contained, opt-in T2 backend (pyright) implements the v1 seam and emits `TIER_T2` evidence
- [ ] Every T2 outcome is `refuted` (trustworthy) or `abstain` (a closed structured reason); no code path
- [ ] With `t2_enabled=false` (the default) the full grounding test suite is byte-identical to pre-epic

## Planned file impact

- `docs/adr/00NN-code-grounding-t2-semantic-resolution.md` (S1, new ADR)
- `src/rebar/grounding/semantic.py` (S2, new T2 dispatch seam)
- `src/rebar/grounding/resolve.py` (S2, `GroundingConfig` + `load_config` T2 keys)
- `src/rebar/grounding/oracle.py` (S2, escalation + `_backend_availability`)
- `src/rebar/grounding/pyright_backend.py` (S3, the pyright backend)
- `pyproject.toml` (S3, `grounding-t2` optional extra)
- `docs/grounding.md` (S3, T2 section + config keys)
- `tests/unit/grounding/` (S2 regression + S3 fail-open matrix)
baseline.summary: Code-grounding T2: self-contained semantic-resolution backends behind the abstain-by-default seam (LSP-lib / compiler-CLI / containerized)

Discovered by the sibling sweep while fixing 12e4 (a stalled snapshot fetch burned the full 300s `_GIT_TIMEOUT`).

12e4 fixed the snapshot path: `_snapshot/git_fetch.fetch_origin` and `repo_snapshot._ensure_blobs_present` now pass `http.lowSpeedLimit`/`http.lowSpeedTime`, so a byte-starved transfer aborts on throughput in ~10s instead of at the wall-clock ceiling.

Three other NETWORK git calls still carry a 300s wall-clock bound and no low-speed abort, so each has the identical exposure:

- `src/rebar/review_bot/gerrit_client.py:367` (and the fetch at :401) — the review bot's own fetch of the Gerrit change, `_GIT_TIMEOUT = 300`. Closest sibling: same process, same per-review budget.
- `src/rebar/opcert_service/workspace.py:107,124` — `fetch --quiet review|tickets`, `_GIT_TIMEOUT = 300`.
- `src/rebar/_commands/init.py:398,419` — `_FETCH_TIMEOUT = 300`.

Deliberately NOT in scope for 12e4: they are a different remote (self-hosted Gerrit) or a different command path, no stall has been measured on them, and folding them in would have widened an already-large change that was forced to split a module. The 30s callers (`_store/push.py`, `_store/sync.py`, `_store/event_append.py`, `_ref_lock.py`) are low value — 30s is already an order of magnitude tighter than the observed stall.

Reuse the seam 12e4 built: `rebar._snapshot.git_fetch.stall_abort_args()` and `is_stall_abort()` are module-public and take no snapshot-specific state, so each call site is a splice of `*stall_abort_args()` before the subcommand plus a decision about whether to retry.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] Each of the three 300s network fetch sites passes the low-speed options.
- [ ] A test per site proves a zero-byte remote aborts as a stall, and that a dribbling remote is not aborted.
- [ ] No new duplicate of the abort logic: the sites reuse `git_fetch.stall_abort_args()`.
baseline.summary: Arm the throughput-keyed stall abort on the remaining 300s git fetches

baseline.description:
## What
`rebar review-code` assembles its diff with a TWO-dot range `git diff base..head`
(`src/rebar/llm/code_review/assemble.py`). When `head` is behind `base` (reviewing a PR branch
not caught up to `origin/main`), a two-dot diff shows `head` relative to base's CURRENT tip, so
every commit merged into `base` since the branch point appears as a spurious deletion. This
inflates the review with a revert of unrelated work and produces phantom-deletion findings that
cite real line numbers but describe changes the PR never made. Reported upstream from a client
project: a 7-file PR reviewed as 11 files with ~720 phantom deletions; 3 of 5 findings were
artifacts.

## Approach
Switch both diff invocations in `assemble_diff_context` from `base..head` to the THREE-dot
`base...head` (merge-base) form, matching git's own PR-review convention. Three-dot diffs `head`
against the merge-base of base and head, excluding unrelated commits on `base` after the branch
point. The change is limited to the `diff_text is None` git path; the supplied-`diff_text` offline
seam is unaffected.

## Scope / files
- `src/rebar/llm/code_review/assemble.py` — two `_git` diff calls (`diff` and `diff --name-only`).
- `tests/unit/test_code_review_assemble.py` — new behavioral regression test.

## Acceptance criteria
- A branch behind its base reviews ONLY the branch's own changed files; commits merged into base
  after the branch point are not surfaced as deletions.
- New regression test `test_diff_is_merge_base_three_dot_not_two_dot` builds a real repo with a
  branch behind main and asserts `changed_files == ["feat.py"]` (no phantom `other.py`); it fails
  under two-dot and passes under three-dot.
- lint, typecheck, and the assemble test module stay green.

## Out of scope
Run-to-run non-determinism and the supply-chain/severity findings from the same upstream report
are tracked separately.
baseline.summary: code-review --base uses two-dot diff; reviewing a branch behind base surfaces phantom deletions

baseline.description:
## Context / Problem
Running `uv` in this checkout generates a `uv.lock` at the repo root that shows up as an untracked file. rebar deliberately keeps core dependencies unpinned (`>=`), and `.github/dependabot.yml` states a `uv` ecosystem block should be added only "if a uv.lock is ever committed" — so the lockfile is a per-developer artifact that must not be tracked.

## Approach
Add a `uv.lock` entry to `.gitignore` with an explanatory comment matching the file's existing commented style, placed alongside the other per-developer tooling ignore rules (e.g. `.serena/`, `.tokensave/`). No dependency-manifest change — core deps stay unpinned `>=` by design; this only stops an already-uncommitted artifact from appearing as untracked.

## Scope
- `.gitignore` — add a commented `uv.lock` ignore rule.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] `.gitignore` contains a `uv.lock` rule; verified by `git check-ignore uv.lock` printing `uv.lock` and exiting 0.
- [ ] A stray root `uv.lock` no longer appears in `git status --porcelain`.
- [ ] No other tracked files change; verified by `git diff --stat` on the change showing only `.gitignore`.
baseline.summary: Ignore per-developer uv.lock in .gitignore

baseline.description:
# S5 — Trusted-proxy passthrough verifier

## Why
Many organizations terminate authentication at an edge proxy / gateway (oauth2-proxy, API Gateway,
ALB) and want the backend to trust the already-authenticated identity — and it is the only in-scope
path for identity systems that are not token issuers (e.g. GitHub-user via oauth2-proxy). This
verifier lets rebar delegate auth to that fronting proxy safely, through the SAME composite contract
as token verifiers.

## What
Add a **trusted-proxy** mode to `src/rebar/_mcp_auth.py`, activated by including `proxy` in the `mcp.auth_strategies` list (the strategy-selection
config key **introduced by S2**, this story's dependency — not a pre-existing seam), with flat config keys it registers: `auth_proxy_secret_env` (NAME of an env
var holding the proxy shared secret — no plaintext secret in config), `auth_proxy_secret_header`
(default `x-proxy-auth`), `auth_proxy_identity_header` (default `x-forwarded-user`), and
`auth_proxy_scopes` (comma-separated fixed scope set granted to proxy-authenticated principals;
OPTIONAL, defaults to an EMPTY set — a proxy-authenticated principal then holds no scopes and is
denied 403 by any non-empty `auth_required_scopes` until scopes are configured). It
comprises a small ASGI middleware plus a `TokenVerifier`-shaped component so that proxy identity
flows through the **same composite**, not around it:
- The **middleware** runs before the MCP app: it validates the shared-secret header (constant-time)
  and, only if valid, extracts the identity header into a request-scoped principal; otherwise it
  strips it. It **strips the entire `X-Forwarded-*` family** (and the configured identity/secret
  headers) from any inbound request that does not present the valid secret, normalizing header-name
  case and underscore/dash variants to defeat smuggling.
- The **verifier** turns that verified request-scoped identity into an `AccessToken` with
  `client_id`=the identity, `scopes`=`auth_proxy_scopes`, and **`resource=auth_resource_server_url`**
  so it passes the composite audience check exactly like a token verifier. If no verified proxy
  identity is present it returns None (composite falls through / denies) — it never accepts on a
  missing/invalid secret.
- **Ordering:** the proxy verifier participates in the composite `auth_strategies` order like any
  other; a bare request with no valid proxy identity is not accepted by it, so a co-configured bearer
  verifier still gets its turn. Adds the `auth_proxy_*` fields to `McpConfig`/`_SECTIONS['mcp']` (`src/rebar/_config_schema.py`); their derived `REBAR_MCP_AUTH_PROXY_*` env-var names go in `MCP_ENV_VARS` (`src/rebar/mcp_server.py`) + `server.json`; `scripts/check_server_manifest.py` passes (docs regenerated by S7).

## Approach & rationale
Implement the oauth2-proxy-blessed trusted-header pattern, and route the result through the composite
(not around it) so the single audience/fail-closed choke point (S2) still applies. Bind HTTP to
loopback (S1 default) so only the proxy can reach the server; require a proxy shared secret; strip
any inbound identity/forwarded headers unless the secret is valid. This is the documented mitigation
for the forwarded-header-spoofing class (oauth2-proxy CVE-2026-40575 / CVE-2025-64484). A tiny ASGI
middleware is the right seam because forwarded identity lives on headers the token-only
`verify_token` seam does not see.

## Scope
The trusted-proxy verifier + its header-guard middleware only, on the S2 seam. Subset of the epic.
Depends on S2. Independent of S3/S4/S6.

## Security
Boundary-crossing and itself a spoofing surface. Hard requirements:
- **Loopback bind** is the intended deployment (S1 default); a non-loopback bind is governed by S1's
  existing non-loopback gate (both allowlists + TLS-at-edge ack) — no new bind key.
- **Operator prerequisite (documented, loud):** the fronting proxy MUST overwrite/strip all
  client-supplied identity and forwarded headers before adding its own; rebar additionally strips the
  entire `X-Forwarded-*` family on its side unless the shared secret validates.
- The env var named by `auth_proxy_secret_env` MUST be present and non-empty at startup or the proxy
  verifier refuses to start (fail-closed).
- The shared secret proves "from the proxy," not identity authenticity — so identity is trusted ONLY
  when the secret validates AND the header survived rebar's strip-then-repopulate; a constant-time
  compare gates it; header-name normalization defeats underscore/case smuggling.
- The minted `AccessToken` carries `resource=auth_resource_server_url`, so it is still subject to the
  composite audience check; fail-closed (no valid secret → no identity → 401).

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] The `auth_proxy_*` config fields exist in `McpConfig`/`_SECTIONS['mcp']` (`_config_schema.py`);
      their derived `REBAR_MCP_AUTH_PROXY_*` env-var names are in `MCP_ENV_VARS` (`mcp_server.py`) +
      `server.json`; and `scripts/check_server_manifest.py` passes (observable oracle: manifest drift
      test green; both files contain the new env-var names). Docs regenerated by S7.
- [ ] Unit test (tier: unit — the ASGI middleware + verifier exercised directly) asserts: with a
      valid `auth_proxy_secret` header, the identity header yields an `AccessToken` whose
      `client_id`=identity, `scopes`=`auth_proxy_scopes`, and `resource==auth_resource_server_url`;
      without the secret, the identity header is stripped and the request is unauthenticated (401).
- [ ] Unit test asserts a client cannot spoof identity: sending `x-forwarded-user` (or the
      underscore/case variants `X_Forwarded_User`, `X-FORWARDED-USER`) directly WITHOUT the valid
      secret is stripped and never trusted; and that the entire `X-Forwarded-*` family is stripped in
      that case (negative controls for each variant).
- [ ] Unit test asserts the verifier refuses to start when the env var named by `auth_proxy_secret_env`
      is absent or empty (observable oracle: startup raises a clear message).
- [ ] Unit test asserts `auth_proxy_scopes` defaults to an empty set when unset, so a valid proxy
      principal holds no scopes and is denied 403 by a non-empty `auth_required_scopes` (observable
      oracle: 403 with empty proxy scopes vs 200 once the required scope is granted).
- [ ] Integration test (httpx `ASGITransport`) asserts an authenticated proxy request (valid secret +
      identity header) → 200, and that the proxy-minted token still passes the composite audience
      check; a bare request → 401.
- [ ] Integration test asserts composition: with `auth_strategies=proxy,static`, a request with no
      proxy identity but a valid static token still succeeds (proxy verifier returns None, static
      accepts) — observable oracle: 200.
- [ ] `make lint && make typecheck && make test` pass.

## Compatibility
Additive, opt-in via the `proxy` strategy. No change to other verifiers or the stdio path.
baseline.summary: S5 — Trusted-proxy passthrough verifier

content.text: The snapshot janitor never garbage-collects the new pinned ticket-store cache entries (`<store>/tickets-<sha>/`) introduced in PR #67, so they accumulate unboundedly as the `tickets` branch changes — a local-disk leak in the gate snapshot cache. They are also absent from the janitor's byte-total accounting.
## Reproduction Steps
1. Run the plan-review / completion gates repeatedly while the `tickets` branch HEAD changes between runs (normal: every ticket write advances it).
2. Each distinct tickets SHA materializes a fresh `<store>/tickets-<sha>/.tickets-tracker/` copy of the whole ticket store.
3. Inspect the snapshot store (`REBAR_GATE_TMPDIR` / `store_root()`): the `tickets-<sha>` dirs accumulate and are never evicted.
## Expected vs Actual
- Expected: the janitor evicts stale `tickets-<sha>` entries by the same grace/LRU/size policy it applies to code-snapshot `<sha>` entries, and counts them in the byte total.

- Actual: `src/rebar/_snapshot/janitor.py:_is_entry` treats an entry as `all(c in "0123456789abcdef" for c in name)` — the `tickets-` prefix is non-hex, so `_is_entry("tickets-<sha>")` is False. `_entries()` therefore excludes them: they are never evicted (leak) and never counted (under-reported cache size).
## Root Cause
`_is_entry` (janitor.py) recognizes only all-hex directory names; PR #67's `tickets-<sha>` entries don't match.
## Fix direction

Extend `_is_entry` to also recognize `tickets-<40hex>` (e.g. accept names matching `^(tickets-)?[0-9a-f]{40}$`), so `_entries()` includes them for eviction + accounting. Verify `_evict`/`_remove_sidecars` behave for a `tickets-`-named entry (no caveats sidecar — the unlink is try/except, harmless). Add a janitor test that a stale `tickets-<sha>` entry is evicted past the grace window.
## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] `_is_entry` returns True for a `tickets-<40hex>` dir; `_entries()` includes it.
- [ ] The janitor evicts a stale `tickets-<sha>` entry (past grace) and counts it in the byte total.
- [ ] A regression test covers eviction + accounting of a `tickets-<sha>` entry.
- [ ] Code-snapshot `<sha>` entry handling is unchanged.
- [ ] Fix lands via PR to main.

baseline.summary: snapshot janitor leaks pinned ticket-store entries (tickets-<sha> not GC'd)

## Summary
Three tests pass locally (uncontended) but fail intermittently under loaded CI runners, blocking the Gerrit Verified gate and forcing repeated rechecks (observed 4+ times in one session). Each has a specific, changeable root cause — not generic 'flakiness'.

## Root causes (confirmed by reading + local repro)
1. **tests/scripts/graph/test_graph_perf.py::test_graph_build_scales_linearly** — asserts algorithmic complexity via WALL-CLOCK ratio t(2N)/t(N) < 3.0. The ratio only cancels UNIFORM load; a transient pause during one of the two sequential measurements skews it (observed 3.26, 4.44). REDUNDANT: the same file's deterministic call-count tests (test_build_dep_graph_single_batch_scan asserts exactly 1 reduce_all_tickets call; test_find_direct_blockers_no_per_ticket_scan / test_compute_dep_graph_children_use_preloaded_state assert 0 rescans) already lock the O(n) invariant. (test_hierarchy_enforcement_benchmark_relative is the same wall-clock-ratio class, latent.)
2. **tests/unit/grounding/test_harness.py::test_worker_hard_crash_maps_to_parse_error_not_host_crash** — in src/rebar/grounding/harness.py run_in_worker, the branch 'if payload is None and proc.is_alive(): return timeout' (line ~341) is racy: on SIGABRT the pipe closes (poll returns EOF, payload=None) but the just-killed child may not be reaped yet, so is_alive() transiently returns True -> misclassified 'timeout' instead of falling through to exitcode<0 -> 'parse_error' (line ~359). Correct discriminator is whether poll(call_timeout) TIMED OUT (still working) vs returned readable/EOF (exited/crashed). Violates the docstring contract (lines 287-288) + the test.
3. **tests/unit/rebar_reconciler/state/test_acli_subprocess_timeout.py::test_run_acli_429_retries_with_rate_limit_backoff** — patches acli_subprocess.time.sleep (the GLOBAL time module) and asserts delays == [1.0]. acli's own two sleep sites produce 2s/4s/Retry-After values, so the observed extra 0.001..0.05 series comes from OTHER code (a reap/poll loop) via the over-broad global patch; count is nondeterministic under load. Fix scopes the assertion to the retry backoff, not all process sleeps.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] The three tests are deterministic — assert invariants/behavior, not wall-clock or global sleep counts — and cannot fail from runner contention.
- [ ] harness.run_in_worker classifies a signal-killed worker as parse_error regardless of reap timing; a RED test reproduces the misclassification deterministically (inject the is_alive race) and passes after the fix; mutation (revert) returns it to RED.
- [ ] The O(n) build invariant remains covered by the deterministic call-count tests after the wall-clock tests are removed/demoted; genuine perf/benchmark checks do not gate the merge.
- [ ] The acli 429 test asserts exactly the Retry-After backoff behavior, robust to unrelated process-reap sleeps.
- [ ] make lint && make typecheck && make test green.
baseline.summary: CI flakes: three merge-gating tests fail under loaded runners (wall-clock/timing/over-broad mock), forcing rechecks

# S9 — ADR + documentation for the provider seam and the two-tier support policy

## Context / Problem

After S1–S8 rebar has a provider seam, a tier policy, a Bedrock path, and tier-stamped verdicts — none of it written down. `docs/llm-framework.md:121-143` still describes provider support as "pydantic-ai resolves the provider from the model string" with no mention of tiers, Bedrock, or what a best-effort provider means for a signed verdict, and its `:131-133` local-server recipe describes behavior that only becomes true in S4. Without a recorded decision, the next Bedrock/gateway request reopens the same argument as a one-off, which is the failure mode this epic exists to end.

## Approach

Write one ADR recording the decisions and, importantly, the rejected alternatives with their evidence: the seam is pydantic-ai's `provider_factory` hook and capabilities come from `ModelProfile`; two support tiers with Anthropic and Bedrock first-class; native Bedrock rather than a gateway; LiteLLM rejected as an in-process dependency but reachable as a proxy; verdicts sign on every tier but stamp the tier. Then bring `docs/llm-framework.md` in line with what the code now does, including the Bedrock recipe, the tier table, and what tier means for an attestation consumer.

The ADR also records the two operational findings this epic turned up, so they are not rediscovered: the IMDS hop-limit constraint and its containment [rebar:9249-1569-7be9-4f67], and the measured relationship between cross-region inference profiles and prompt caching [rebar:2932-8a98-6d70-4550].

**Alternative rejected:** documenting in `docs/llm-framework.md` only. That records the *what* but not the *why*, and rebar's ADR set is where rejected alternatives live — without them the LiteLLM and gateway options get re-proposed.

## Scope

- `docs/adr/00NN-llm-provider-seam-and-support-tiers.md` (new).
- `docs/llm-framework.md` — the provider section (`:121-143`) and the env table (`:224-226`).
- `docs/env-vars.md` — regenerated.
- `README.md` — one line if the provider story is summarized there.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [x] the ADR exists, is `Accepted`, and names each rejected alternative (in-process LiteLLM, gateway-fronted

content.text: ## Why

Bin-packing contamination is UNMEASURABLE: the sidecar stamps each finding's criteria but throws away chunk co-residency (only a chunk COUNT survives). Cannot calibrate R-1-part-2 (epic fort-wisp-wren) without measuring it.
## What (verified code targets)

- Stamp each Pass-1 finding with its chunk COHORT (sorted criterion-id set). Findings come from THREE finder paths: pass1_chunk (passes.py def@255) -- multi-criterion chunk, cohort = the chunk's sorted ids; pass1_container (def@310) -- cohort = its container criteria ids; pass1_isf (def@409) -- runs as a SINGLE fixed call (not a multi-criterion chunk), so cohort = a singleton ["ISF"] (define this explicitly; ISF is never co-resident, so its contamination cohort is itself).

- Carry the key through _slim (sidecar.py def@228). CORRECTION: _slim uses an explicit key-ALLOWLIST return dict and deliberately excludes runtime-only carriers -- cohort must be ADDED to that allowlist or it is stripped. cohort is a small scalar list, safe to persist.
- Old sidecars / pre-change findings lack cohort: offline analysis must treat a MISSING cohort as "unknown" (skip from the contamination rate), not empty. State this fallback.

- Out-of-plan_review callers of the finding shape: src/rebar/llm/evals/eval_solver.py (~line 100) and src/rebar/llm/workflow/criterion_preview.py (~line 365) call pass1_chunk -- confirm they tolerate the extra key.
- Document the cohort field in a sidecar schema note (docs).
## Provenance

Gap-report labels (G-*/FP-*/R-*/WS-N) are tags from ~/dso_rebar_plan_review_gap_report.md + session log brief-bride-rash (95f1-1b3b-a867-4020), NOT codebase symbols. Symbols introduced by a SIBLING story (e.g. committed_work_relies_on_unbacked_claim from WS1) are target-state, not pre-existing; the dependency is recorded.
## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] cohort (sorted chunk criterion-id set; ISF singleton ["ISF"]) stamped on findings from pass1_chunk AND pass1_container AND pass1_isf, and added to _slim's allowlist. Proof: run a minimal review; `jq '.findings[].cohort' <sidecar>` non-null for all three finder types; author cases in tests/unit/test_sidecar_enrichment.py (the ACTUAL sidecar test file) asserting cohort content correctness; `pytest tests/unit/test_sidecar_enrichment.py -k cohort` green.
- [ ] Sidecar schema note added for cohort; offline analysis treats missing cohort as unknown (documented).
- [ ] Both out-of-tree callers (eval_solver.py, criterion_preview.py) still pass. Proof: their existing tests green.
- [ ] A small script/query computes a blocking-tier contamination rate from cohort data (committed under scripts/ or a test). Unblocks fort-wisp-wren.
